Live Science spoke with Nobel laureate Francis Halzen on how he got into physics "by accident" and built a neutrino detector that changed it forever.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Francis Halzen first proposed burying a $271 million telescope deep beneath the South Pole, he expected to be laughed off stage. Four decades later, it won him a Nobel Prize.

Consisting of thousands of light sensors strung like rosary beads inside a cubic kilometer (0.2 cubic miles) of pristine ice, his detector, aptly named IceCube, is not an obvious way to study the universe. But Halzen, a theoretical physicist at the University of Madison-Wisconsin, isn't looking for something obvious.

His quarries are neutrinos, near-massless, chargeless, shapeshifters that are the most abundant material particles in existence. They form from nuclear processes and high-energy collisions, swarming out of our sun and whizzing from the outskirts of black holes. Yet though neutrinos stream through stars, planets, and us every second in their trillions, you still have a 75% chance of living your entire life without a single one striking an atom in your body.

On the rare occasions neutrinos do interact with atoms, they create charged particles that zip through water or ice faster than light does, casting a faint blue cone — the optical equivalent of a sonic boom.

Since 2011, IceCube has been retracing this blue light to study neutrinos produced by the most violent astrophysical events, probing energies far beyond those of Earth-based laboratories to find cracks in the laws of physics.

In the wake of his Nobel win, Live Science sat down with Halzen to discuss neutrinos, IceCube's journey from fanciful proposal to historic success, and the future of mapping the cosmos using the trails of ghosts. Here's what he had to say.

Ben Turner: What first got you into physics?

Francis Halzen: I got into physics kind of by accident. When I came out of high school, I didn't know what to do. I was interested in languages, I was interested in science. I'm a bad example of an inspirational career.

Francis Halzen is a Belgian-American particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madinson who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. Halzen first proposed the telescope's prototype, called AMANDA, in 1988.

I did mathematics because in the Belgian system it was very much in the old French style — in fact, it was created by Napoleon — and hadn't changed when I was in high school. And so, if you were a good student, mathematics was the thing to do, right? So I did mathematics for two years, and then I did physics in parallel, and then switched to physics. When I switched, I got a professor who became my supervisor and he gave me the paper of George Zweig [who co-proposed quarks alongside Murray Gell-Mann] on quarks, which was a fundamental discovery.

George Zweig was actually an experimentalist, and he made these calculations using little figures. I recognized, as I had done mathematics, that this was group theory; and I said "I can do this better." I actually wrote several papers on the subject; and so suddenly I was a theoretical particle physicist. And that's what I still am. My heart never left particle physics.

BT: And then quarks eventually became neutrinos for you. Why neutrinos?

FH: I actually didn't study neutrinos until I really got involved in starting this experiment. Half of my career, which was passed by the time I started AMANDA [IceCube's prototype] and IceCube, I really had very little overlap with neutrino physics.

I became interested in neutrinos again [while] solving a theoretical problem. In fact, the idea of detecting neutrinos with ice originated with [Gurgen] Askaryan, an Armenian physicist, in 1963.

You cannot see neutrinos. They have no charge. They have basically no mass. So the way to detect neutrinos is when they interact with the nucleus. We are moving now in a sea of neutrinos, but neutrinos don't interact with atoms, so we don't know it. But if they accidentally hit the nucleus of an atom, then they make a nuclear reaction, and that emits charged particles. It's like a spark, and you can detect a spark with antennas.

So Askaryan's idea was to put radio antennas in ice. We are doing exactly that. But instead of looking at the radio emission, we look at the light that's emitted, which is just blue light. We use that blue light to reconstruct the neutrino and all its properties, including its direction — [that's] why it is a telescope, right?

Building on Askaryan's idea, The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA) complements IceCube by searching for high-energy neutrinos with radio antennas buried 200 meters (670 feet) below Antarctica's ice.

I was worrying about that experiment because they had not been able to calculate the power of the spark, so they didn't know if this worked or not. Then someone told me at some point that the Russians — I guess it was still the Soviet Union — are actually doing this at a station in Antarctica by pointing [radio] dishes into the ice. I said: "This is crazy."

But I had ice all over my brain, right? When I saw in the late 80s how difficult it was to do these experiments in deep ocean water it was normal to have the idea to do it in ice. And, to our credit, we understood that it actually may be simpler.

BT: Why is being able to calculate the power of the spark so important?

FH: [It's about] how much light is made, and how far it travels through your detector. If you don't make enough light, and it's immediately absorbed, then you have no experiment.

The reason we are talking to each other [today] is because we had this incredible luck that blue light travels 100 meters [328 feet] and more through this ancient ice without being absorbed. So it's relatively easy to instrument an ice block of a kilometer cubed with light sensors.

BT: When you first proposed melting 61 two-kilometre [1.2-mile] holes in the coldest place on Earth, you said you expected to be laughed off stage. Then when you weren't, you said you continued to worry about it. What were you worrying about?

FH: Well, the worry was that I was totally out of my league. I didn't understand glaciology, I am not an experimentalist, so I didn't really grasp the technological challenges of doing this. The experiments in water were not doing very well: There was the leading experiment off the coast of Hawaii [the Deep Underwater Muon And Neutrino Detector, or DUMAND, project] and it happened that the man leading this experiment, John Learned, was a good friend of mine, and I eventually contacted him.

And the glaciology, of course. Nobody knew what the optical properties were of ice at a depth of one kilometer [0.6 miles] or more under the South Pole. There were [ice] cores that had been taken, but cores are small — the size of a teacup — so you cannot tell how far the light travels [through the ice]. So people thought it was a cute idea that would never work.

If I had known more about glaciology, about hot water drilling, and about the technical challenges, I would never have started this experiment. It's the advantage of being ignorant. It's why young people make great discoveries, and when you're 82 years old you don't make this progress — you know too much.

An artist's illustration showing what the interior of IceCube would look like without the ice.

BT: You speak about AMANDA and IceCube with a lot of ambivalence. You said you "got dragged into it by accident" and "tried to get out of it many times."

FH: Oh yes, absolutely. You know, theorists write two types of papers: [the first are] papers where they think they contribute to the progress of science — they usually don't. But the other type of paper is just to show you're smart. And this was definitely in the second category. And then two people from Berkeley [Doug Lowder and Andrew Westphal] actually started the experiment.

BT: Well, you won a Nobel Prize for it. If you wanted to look smart, you succeeded.

FH: Yeah, without a lot of luck, I wouldn't be sitting here.

They're this almost non-existent piece of reality.

BT: But surely it wasn't just showing off? Despite all of the uncertainties and worries, there must have been something about neutrinos — these barely detectable, misbehaving particles — that's so important it made you stick around. What's the draw to learn about them?

FH: Neutrinos are something really special, right? When you look at the Standard Model of matter [which describes all the known particles and forces], it has quarks, leptons, and neutrinos.

But neutrinos are special in the sense that they're supposed to have no mass. They're just like photons: they travel at the speed of light, so you can do astronomy with them. But then they have the advantage that they go through planets; they go through the Earth; they reach you from the beginning of time; they reach you from the edge of the universe. They're this almost non-existent piece of reality.

So they always had a special fascination. We knew they existed since 1930; because without neutrinos you cannot change a proton into a neutron. They were ghosts — that's where the name "ghost particle" comes from. They were part of physics, and particle physics, and nuclear physics, but they had never been seen.

It's only in 1956 that [Frederick] Reines and [Clyde] Cowen finally discovered the neutrino by putting a detector close to a nuclear reactor, where there are lots of them. If they don't interact, then you compensate by going to a place where there are lots of them, and a nuclear reactor was an opportunity.

It's a fascinating particle. Of course now it fascinates us because they do have mass, which is not allowed by the structure of the Standard Model, and so they carry some information on new physics — the new physics we are looking for with the Large Hadron Collider in Geneva. They are the particles that have carried the message of that new physics most directly, and that's our domain.

We should have all the advantages. Sadly, they just behave like the Standard Model in everything we have done over the first 15 years of this experiment.

Construction workers inside one of the two colossal caverns created for the particle detector modules of Fermilab's Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). By probing the properties of neutrinos, physicists are hoping to assess key theories, including neutrinos' hypothesized role in tipping the universe into containing more matter than antimatter.

BT: Famously, in 1993 to '94, microscopic air bubbles trapped in Antarctica's ice scattered neutrinos' blue light like frosted glass, nearly killing the project. You saved it by drilling to where the ice sheet's weight crushed those bubbles out of existence, up to 2.5 kilometers [1.6 miles] beneath the surface and one kilometer deeper than you originally planned. How hard was that?

FH: Well, the drilling almost killed the project twice.

It's actually an interesting story, because we now detect a neutrino every minute as we are speaking, but they are produced in the atmosphere. They [atmospheric neutrinos] are our background — interesting background, but a background.

As energetic particles called cosmic rays strike Earth's upper atmosphere, they create showers of smaller particles, including neutrinos, that can be detected on the surface. IceCube's scientists filter out lower-energy atmospheric neutrinos (alongside those produced by the sun) to find only those made in astrophysical cataclysms.

After we had solved all these problems and could detect neutrinos, the only threshold to cross was to produce a drill that could build IceCube. That involves melting ice over two and a half kilometers over an area the size of a basketball. The technique existed in glaciers, but [produced] a shallow hole about the size of a bottle of wine.

So we went to companies specialized in building hoses, and we needed a hose that was 2.5 kilometers long. The first company we went to told us: "Look, you hang a hose the size of a tea cup over two and a half kilometers of hot water and what do you think will happen?" It will collapse. Even the theorists could understand that it would collapse.

And that was the end of the project. For weeks I thought it was finished. I told one of our engineers, a brilliant guy who contributed much more than what I'm going to tell you, and he didn't give up. He found a company in Padua, Italy, near Venice and they said: "We can build anything." And they did.

Then, when we started drilling, it was still a problem. We drilled one hole over a whole [South Pole] season. We had brilliant engineers working on this totally new piece of equipment — you have no idea how complex this is — and they learned from the mistakes of the first year and the second year it worked. They deployed 86 strings without ever failing, which is amazing actually. It's like when you launch 86 satellites, you're probably going to fail some. That's what we thought. But they never did.

A view down along one of IceCube's 86 detector strings, dangling in holes drilled up to 2.5 kilometers into the ice.

BT: The detector went online in 2011, then that year and the next came "Bert" and "Ernie" — the first ever detections of astrophysical neutrinos from beyond our solar system. After all that effort, all those near misses, and every doubt you ever had, what did it feel like when they arrived?

FH: We were not sure we believed it. It was clear then that this was a major discovery — if it was true. It took us six months or more to have the courage to write the paper.

I remember seeing the first events on my screen in October of 2012, and they looked like they couldn't have come from the atmosphere — such high energy! We discovered the first two serendipitously in the first two years of data. Then, after we went to look for more knowing what these events look like, we had 28. So we had the courage to publish.

But then, three weeks later, we were declared the physics breakthrough of the year. I must say I was not happy about that. I had to give a press conference, and I was all the time thinking: "If this is not true, how am I going to walk this back?"

It took me quite a while to convince myself that this wasn't just something that looked like cosmic neutrinos. But this is such an unusual corner of science, you don't know whether you are fooled by some other phenomena you haven't thought of.

FH: Well now we are seeing sources of neutrinos. You see 100 neutrinos come from an active galaxy, and you point [a different telescope] back at it with 0.04 degree resolution. There's no doubt now. But being convinced was a continuous process; at least in my case. My colleagues always refer to me as a total optimist, but it took me some time. I was not my usual self on this.

But now there's no doubt. The statistics of observing cosmic neutrinos is totally impossible [to deny] with the precision we have now. But we're talking about 14 years of data. It's really incredible how quickly we've progressed.

A crane deploys the Baikal-GVD neutrino telescope from the ice cover of Lake Baikal, Siberia.

And you realize that, officially, none of the things we see have been confirmed by someone else. There are two experiments, [Baikal-G in Lake Baikal and [KM3NeT] in the Mediterranean Sea, but they're under construction. And they both have produced some kind of evidence, but a real confirmation of seeing the same thing we see has still not happened. So the Nobel Prize [Committee] had more courage than me.

I had forgotten that it was Nobel season.

BT: You were in a hotel room in Italy when the call came from Stockholm. What went through your mind in the first quiet moments after hanging up?

FH: Well, after hanging up, I was sent a Zoom link, and they asked me questions, which I answered. But I didn't know that I was actually giving a press conference. I still haven't looked back at that press conference.

But that's how crazy it was, because I had forgotten that it was Nobel season. The call came by total surprise. Well, it wasn't a total surprise because there's a game of predicting the Nobel Prizes. And I had been there [in the running to win] for several years.

So I cannot say that I was unaware of this. But this was a difficult season for me, right? People literally would send me condolence messages every year for not winning. And they meant it — they're my friends — but it makes you feel strange. You feel you've disappointed your collaborators.

So that's the first thing I thought: "Okay, the problem is solved now. Everybody can get credit for this experiment." And deservedly. Because IceCube was becoming mostly me, and data and science. The fact of its history and the contributions people made was being forgotten very fast. The great thing about this Nobel Prize is that it's for a difficult problem that was solved by so many brilliant people over almost four decades.

BT: Aside from winning the Nobel, what's been the highlight of working on IceCube?

FH: The highlight for me was to show that the technique works. Seeing these neutrinos go through the Earth, and then through the detector, was incredibly exciting because there was no doubt you were looking at a stream of particles going through your detector initiated by neutrinos that came through the Earth. There was no doubt. What you see is what you get.

We had this attitude that if you build something this big you're going to do interesting science. This is so different from anything that has been built before. I don't want to insult astronomers, but our joke was: "We are all particle physicists, guys. God forbid we have to do astronomy." But that's what we are doing.

I must say, it's very, very exciting to learn astronomy when you're 82 years old.

BT: IceCube–Gen2 is targeted to come online by 2033 and will be eight times larger than the original detector. What do you want for its future?

FH: Whenever I give a talk, I have a list of conclusions, and my first is always that neutrino astronomy exists, and that's our contribution. Doing neutrino astronomy will require more instruments, bigger instruments. In astronomy there's not just one telescope, right? To do real astronomy we'll need more instruments covering the sky completely, and we'll need more neutrinos with better angular resolution.

The nice thing is that will happen: There are ambitious projects in China now, and [the upgrade of] our own project too. How can you pass it up? Because now the technology is much better: we understand the ice perfectly; we can design this detector, optimize it, and gain an order of magnitude [improvement] for the same cost as the original.

China's Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) detector while it was under construction in 2024. The detector, which is designed to probe neutrinos from space and from Earth, came online in August 2026.

BT: You famously don't like to make predictions, even one year ahead, about what we might learn about neutrinos. So I'm going to try to be sly with this final question: What do you hope the future has in store for neutrino astronomy?

FH: I hope for a galactic supernova [within the Milky Way]. I don't know if you know the history, but in 1987 there was a supernova in a [nearby] satellite galaxy, but it [meant physicists] detected 20 neutrinos. And what we learned from these neutrinos is incredible — literally thousands of papers have been written about those 20 neutrinos, and they're all interesting.

Neutrinos are supposed to have no mass and be just like photons. The best limit we could set on the [tiny and still unexplained] mass of the neutrino came from that supernova. So we made very fundamental measurements that we hadn't been able to make with [laboratory] neutrino beams. And then the whole story that a star really collapses into a neutron star. All that suddenly became reality. I was not, and am still not, an astronomer, but from the point of view of stellar physics this was a major event.

Now, instead of three experiments, we have multiple neutrino detectors of all kinds. Some will detect thousands of neutrinos; we'll detect a million neutrinos. We can't actually reconstruct them, but we can make a very detailed movie telling you everything that went on in a supernova while the star collapsed and then exploded. The science we will do from a few seconds of data will be incredible.

I can tell you it hasn't happened since the mid-1990s because we have been looking for it continuously with AMANDA and Ice-Cube. There are supposed to be like two per century. We are due.

Editor's note: This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Ben Turner is the features editor at Live Science. He covers physics and astronomy, among other topics such as tech and climate change. He graduated from University College London with a degree in particle physics before training as a journalist. When he's not writing, Ben enjoys reading literature, playing the guitar and losing at chess.

#6297. ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Big Dig podcast host Ian Coss explores how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy worked together to reform American health care laws

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”

Lily Burton was the Spring 2026 science writing intern at Science News. She holds a bachelor’s degree in Molecular and Cell Biology and Anthropology from UC Berkeley. She also has a Ph.D. in Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics from the University of Chicago where she researched circadian rhythms in photosynthetic bacteria and the role they play in metabolism. She was a 2024 AAAS Mass Media Fellow where she reported on local science at WUNC – North Carolina Public Radio.

Grab the small ratchet when there’s barely enough room to turn your wrist and the larger one when you have more room to break a stubborn nut free. I also like the hard case, which keeps the tools both protected and organized. One look at an empty socket chamber, and I know exactly which one I left beneath my mower deck.

If someone on your holiday list just picked up keys to their first place, I’d get them this set. Leave a drill bit in one tool and a driver in the other, and you can go from drilling pilot holes to running screws without stopping to swap bits. That doesn’t sound like much until you've got an afternoon of hanging curtain rods and shelves in front of you. And I like that the kit includes both tools, two batteries, a charger, and a bag to keep everything together and ready for transport. At $149, this is a perfect entry point into the DeWalt cordless tool ecosystem.

The first time you need to slip a piece of new flooring under a door jamb, you’ll understand exactly why this DeWalt oscillating multitool is one of the most coveted tools in any collection. Trim that jamb right where it sits, without removing it. Same idea if you need to notch a little baseboard in place or make a neat opening in drywall for a new electrical outlet.

Where this deal really shines, however, is the accessories you get with the tool. For $99, you’re also taking home a 4.0 Ah battery, charger, and blade.

If you’re ready to take on that crown molding project you’ve wanted to attempt for so long, this 12-inch sliding miter saw from DeWalt will be your new bestie. The sliding head gives you plenty of room to perform crosscuts on wider boards, and the blade’s shadow line shows exactly where the teeth will land on your measurement. At just over $200 off, this saw is a legacy tool that you’ll likely pass down to the next generation of woodworkers and DIYers in your family.

I love this sander. DeWalt has lowered the overall profile of this new XR sander, so you can reach tight spaces when you need to sand something in place, like the inside of a cabinet. The tool feels great in your palm, and the weight is dead-centered on the pad, which keeps it planted on your work surface. Five speed settings allow you to back off when you’re easing an edge or turn it up when you need serious material removal. At $144, I’d put this one on the Black Friday list for anyone already on the DeWalt platform, as both battery and charger are sold separately.

For many people, a big reciprocating saw is probably too much tool. How much demolition will you actually do? But picture yourself under a sink or in a crawl space trying to cut out an old pipe with your elbows jammed up around your ears. That’s where I’d take this compact DeWalt reciprocating saw over one of those larger ones. With the right blade, you’ll tear through that pipe—or cut the nails holding a broken fence picket and leave the neighboring boards alone. At 63 percent off, you still have plenty left in the budget for a battery and charger.

If I were putting together a cordless tool kit from scratch, I’d start here. The drill and impact driver are the pair I reach for whenever I’m drilling pilot holes and driving fasteners in tandem. The oscillating multitool handles the awkward cuts, like trimming a door jamb so I can install new flooring underneath it or cutting a fast hole in drywall for a new receptacle. With three batteries and a charger included in the bag, you can leave a battery on each tool while you work or keep one in the charger until it’s needed.

If you’re considering any of the cordless tools I’ve mentioned earlier, this Black Friday deal is an easy add. This 5.0 Ah DeWalt battery two-pack makes perfect sense for tools that spend a lot of time in use, like a cordless sander or miter saw. I’ve always been a fan of DeWalt’s easy-access charge gauge on their batteries, which lets you see how much juice you have before you start. Again, this is a great choice if you’re picking up that cordless XR sander, as these batteries have impressive run times, and because this is a two-pack, you can charge one as you work and sand without much downtime.

#6294. Pakistan’s first astronaut heads for China’s space station

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m. EST to launch the Progress MS-36 cargo ship to the International Space Station (ISS) on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, according to Next Spaceflight. NASA still lists the flight only as no earlier than fall 2026 and has not given a date.

At 5:45 a.m. EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites. A problem with the rocket’s ground support systems halted Monday’s countdown. It is Amazon’s first launch since last week’s Vulcan failure.

Later that morning, at 10:55 a.m. EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

That evening, at 7:18 p.m. EST, a Long March 2F is slated to launch Shenzhou-24, carrying three astronauts, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China to the Tiangong space station, per Next Spaceflight.

One seat makes history. A Pakistani astronaut will fly as a payload specialist, becoming the first foreign visitor to Tiangong and Pakistan’s first astronaut. Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), has shortlisted two pilots, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. One will fly and the other will serve as backup. The astronaut is expected to spend about a week on Tiangong and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

On Thursday, Nov. 26, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 4:35 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Thursday, at 7:05 p.m. EST, Rocket Lab will launch Night Owls Never Sleep on an Electron from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula.The payload is a StriX satellite for the Japanese company Synspective. StriX satellites use synthetic aperture radar to image the ground through clouds and darkness.

On Friday, Nov. 27, CASC is targeting 8:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 6A launch from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

On Saturday, Nov. 28, CAS Space, a commercial launch company backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, plans to launch a Kinetica 1 at 8:00 p.m. EST from a sea platform in the South China Sea, supported by the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport, per Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Saturday, at 10:50 p.m. EST, a Long March 6C is slated to lift off from Taiyuan, according to Next Spaceflight. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Finally, at 11:39 p.m. EST on Saturday, SpaceX returns to SLC-4E for USSF-380, another classified Space Force mission. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

Closing out the week on Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the late Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of science and supplies to the ISS.

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:51 p.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from Taiyuan carrying Shijian-24. China has not said what the satellite does; CGTN reported only that it reached its planned orbit.

On Friday, Nov. 20, at 6:59 a.m. EST, a Long March 8A launched from the commercial launch site at Wenchang with the 30th batch of satellites for Guowang, China’s state-backed broadband megaconstellation.

That night, at 11:20 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-317 mission from Vandenberg, two days later than planned. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

The week closed on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 7:23 a.m. EST, when a Falcon 9 lifted off from the same pad with the National Reconnaissance Office’s NROL-136, a day later than planned. The launch came 32 hours after USSF-317, SpaceX’s fastest turnaround between launches from the same pad. The booster flew back to Landing Zone 4.

South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD), the military research arm of its defense ministry, is still preparing the first full demonstration flight of its solid-fueled Mir rocket from an offshore platform near Jeju Island. After canceling a June 30 attempt over safety concerns, the ministry has said only that it aims to launch by the end of the year.

ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), also has a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan on the books no earlier than November 2026. Its payload has not been announced.

A 15th-century shipwreck is yielding clues to the medieval tragedy that destroyed Griffin, King Hans's "floating castle."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have recovered high-quality chain mail armor from the 15th-century wreck of Gribshunden or Griffin, a royal warship that doubled as a "floating castle" for King Hans of Denmark. The ship exploded and sank in 1495, but maritime archaeologists have just begun exploring the area beneath the forecastle, an elevated combat platform at the front of the ship, where they discovered the armor and a unique munitions chest.

The chain mail was, "rather surprisingly, completely exposed," Rolf Warming, an archaeologist at Stockholm University and lead investigator of the Griffin project in collaboration with Södertörn University, told Live Science in an email. "It was only by chance that we came across it, and it shows just how much is still on the wreck site."

The mail armor was made of copper alloy and was found in a part of the ship that may have been used as a storage area for military gear, according to a Nov. 24 statement. "Historical sources indicate that German mercenaries, or Landsknechts, were aboard Griffin when it sank in 1495," Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, an archaeologist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who is the co-investigator on the project, said in the statement. The mercenaries may have stored their armor in the area, "although we've yet to establish a precise function for the space," Pacheco-Ruiz said.

The 15th-century warship was rediscovered in the Baltic Sea off the south coast of Sweden in the 1970s but formally identified by archaeologists as Griffin in 2013.

An X-ray image of the chain mail recovered from the Griffin.

Griffin was the flagship of the naval fleet of King Hans of Denmark and Norway. In 1495, Hans was sailing to Kalmar in Sweden to negotiate a political alliance and force Sweden back into a union with Denmark and Norway. He had brought with him around 150 German mercenary soldiers. "It was important to demonstrate military prowess, and the German and Swiss mercenaries were the finest you could get at that time," Warming told Live Science.

During a stop at the port of Ronneby in what is now Sweden, Griffin caught fire, perhaps after being struck by lightning, and sank. Eyewitnesses who escaped reported that many men died in the tragic event. King Hans, however, was onshore when the warship sank.

The warship has been well-preserved over the centuries thanks to the low salinity of the Baltic waters and the lack of shipworms, marine mollusks also known as the "termites of the sea" because of the damage they do to wood.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The chain mail recovered in October is of exceptionally high quality, Warming said in the statement, but it was not necessarily the armor of an elite knight. "This kind of armour could remain in use for extended periods, often undergoing repairs or being reused, so these fragments may represent older military equipment that was still active," he said.

Archaeologists discovered an unusual munitions chest and chain mail in the medieval shipwreck.

But the researchers discovered more than just the chain mail.

"This year's campaign was an unusually exciting investigation!" Warming told Live Science. The team found a unique munitions chest called a "zeuglade" in German. "We have taken different samples to try to determine the contents of the chest and perhaps find traces of gunpowder," Warming said. The chest may have belonged to the German mercenaries who were aboard.

"It was in the process of documenting the chest that I unexpectedly discovered exposed mail-armour fragments in the vicinity of the chest, along other items that could indicate more chests," Warming added. "This leads us to believe this may have been a stowage area, located just beneath the forecastle."

Warming said that the research team is currently using chemical analysis to investigate the origins of the armor and the chest to learn more about medieval military matters.

"It is probable that the mail armour belongs to the mercenaries, but it could also belong to someone else," Warming said. "The chest might also belong to them, but we don't know yet. It is actually a really fascinating research question of ours that could illuminate supply chains and the military logistics. Did the mercenary forces bring their own ammunition and tool kit aboard, or was this supplied by the royal fleet?"

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

The bright, rapidly rotating star Gamma (γ) Cassiopeiae illuminates two nearby nebula: the reflection nebula IC 59 (below and to the left of the star) and the emission nebula IC 63 (directly below). #6291. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Researchers’ debate shapes how mental health experts advise men

Does “positive masculinity” exist or reinforce sexist gender norms? Researchers grappling with that question say the answer will help determine how doctors and therapists treat men.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their new masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he says. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”

Fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales currently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a new masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”

Such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher says. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”

If you or someone you care about may be at risk of suicide, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers free, 24/7 support, information and local resources from trained counselors. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

#6290. The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 24: A Super Beaver Moon occults the Pleiades

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 23: Double star Kurhah in Cepheus

Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.
