#6157. The Best Galapagos Cruises in 2027 That Combine Luxe Amenities With Rugged Adventure

Visiting the Galapagos can feel like stepping onto another planet. This chain of volcanic islands is a mystical realm of otherworldly lava formations, sweeping oceanic vistas, ancient flora, and endemic animal species not found anywhere else on earth.

This unique archipelago of 20 scattered islands—plus dozens more islets and notable rocks in between—is best explored by a specialty cruise. Sailing through the Galapagos Islands allows travelers the ease of navigating to the destination’s smaller locales, getting up close to rare wildlife, and the constant presence of naturalists who can maximize every moment, from pointing out passing marine life to guided stargazing on deck.

The best Galapagos cruises combine tourism with conservation.

The best Galapagos cruises are intimate voyages aboard specialized ships designed to help preserve the islands’ delicate ecosystems. When the day of intrepid exploring is finished, the ship becomes your floating home, offering travelers a serene space to relax and debrief about the wonders you've just experienced. Here’s a look at the best Galapagos cruises to take in 2027, spanning everything from boutique yachts and all-inclusive cruises to top-of-the-line expedition ships.

This article has been updated with new information since its original publication date.

Ecoventura's Theory is not only luxurious, but it welcomes families (with children ages six and up) with open arms.

For an intimate, curated voyage through the Galapagos, you can’t go wrong with an Ecoventura cruise. The line operates three Relais & Chateaux yachts, Origin, Theory, and Evolve, each of which has just 10 staterooms for a total of 20 guests. Each stateroom offers oversized windows and a sleek, modern design.

Travelers can choose between Ecoventura’s two seven-night itineraries: The “Beaches and Bays” voyage visits San Cristobal, Espanola, Floreana, Santa Cruz, Bartolome, and North Seymour Islands, and the “Volcanic Wonders” sailing calls upon more remote locations like Isabela and Fernandina Islands. (There’s also the option to combine both into a 14-night sailing.)

The line’s expedition guides, who are trained in birdwatching, stargazing, and nature photography, escort travelers to notable locations, like the red sand beach on Rabida Island with its flocks of American Flamingos, and the iconic pinnacle rock of Bartolome Island. There’s also kayaking, zodiac rides, and snorkeling among sea turtles, sea lions, reef fish, and more. Scuba divers can board the line’s 16-passenger luxury vessel, Galapagos Sky, for multi-day dive excursions to seek out whale sharks, hammerheads, and manta rays.

Galápagos sea lions, as seen on a cruise

One of the most luxurious options in the Galapagos, Silversea has brought its lavish, all-inclusive concept to the rugged archipelago aboard its destination-specific ship Silver Origin. The all-suite, all-balcony vessel holds 100 passengers and offers butler service in every suite, plus an in-room bar stocked to your preferences. Each suite is ultra-spacious, but the villa category offers sweeping terraces, vast living spaces and dining areas, and a separate bedroom. Elsewhere on the ship are two restaurants, a lounge, spa, fitness center, and stargazing platform— collectively, a promise that passengers will never be bored.

Silversea’s seven-day Galapagos itineraries all sail round-trip from the island of San Cristobal. Depending on the exact sailing, voyages call upon a wide variety of islands, including Isabela, Fernandina, North Seymour, Santa Cruz, Espanola, and more. With the included excursions, guests can explore the lunar landscapes of Isabela’s ancient lava flows, witness the seabird sanctuaries of Prince Philip's Steps, participate in guided nature hikes, deep-water snorkeling, zodiac cruises, and kayaking. Luxe touches, like free expedition gear and unlimited pours of Champagne on board, push the voyages over the top. Plus, Silver Origin’s specialized features—like a dynamic positioning system and advanced propulsion—are easier on the local ecosystem's fragile marine life.

The National Geographic Gemini hosts some of the best Galapagos cruises for bringing kids along.

Inspire your kids to learn about science and exploration by hopping on board one of Lindblad Expedition's four Galapagos ships: National Geographic Endeavour II, National Geographic Islander II, National Geographic Gemini, and National Geographic Delfina. These journeys, led by National Geographic experts, give kids the chance to become National Geographic Explorers-In-Training. The exclusive, hands-on program is designed to teach kids about geographical exploration and scientific research. The National Geographic Gemini, which launched in 2025, can accommodate up to 48 passengers in 27 suites. More than a dozen suites come with private balconies, and one of those balconies is large enough to accommodate a private hot tub. But don’t fret if that suite is already booked; there’s a whirlpool hot tub on the sundeck that’s open to all guests. There’s also a library, well-stocked bar, and meals made with locally sourced ingredients on board.

andBeyond's 124-foot expedition yacht Galapagos Explorer

With its 124-foot expedition yacht, Galapagos Explorer, andBeyond offers a truly exclusive experience. The yacht has only six rooms to accommodate 12 guests, and it’s also available for a fully private charter. Across the yacht’s four decks are a hot tub, sun deck, swim deck, as well as indoor and outdoor dining rooms and bars. In the five cabins and one larger suite, passengers will find a warm design accented with an oceanic color palette and natural materials like carved wood accents and indigenous textiles—making the ship feel more like a boutique hotel than a cruise. &Beyond’s seven-day itineraries call upon multiple islands either to the east or west, with a mix of popular and more remote locales, like Genovesa, Bartolome, Santa Cruz, Floreana, Espanola, Isabela, and Santa Fe. Snorkeling, kayaking, guided hikes, and island tours are all part of the daily activities with the expedition team, who can personalize each excursion thanks to the small number of guests on board.

The 164-foot superyacht Aqua Mare carries 16 passengers and 16 crew members.

The 164-foot superyacht Aqua Mare is all about bespoke attention. The small vessel carries 16 passengers, with 16 crew members to look after guests’ every need. Within the ship’s elegant interiors are seven cabins with gleaming woodwork, marble-accented bathrooms, and an owner’s suite with multiple bedrooms and living spaces.

Spanning the rest of the yacht’s four decks are a panoramic sundeck, hot tub, and indoor and outdoor dining rooms, where chef Pedro Miguel Schiaffino serves up Peruvian Nikkei-style cuisine. Expect selections like potato llapingachos, tuna crudo, barbecued plantains, and shrimp ceviche created with ingredients sourced from local farmers, fishermen, and other purveyors. The lower-deck swim platform and beach club is the launch point for kayaks, paddle boards, and snorkeling, or lazy days by the water.

Itineraries cover a wide breadth of islands, from the northern reaches of Genovesa to the southernmost Espanola, and Santa Fe, Santa Cruz, and Santiago in between. Western-focused itineraries arc around the far West side of Isabela Island, which allows for rarefied activities. Guests can hike among the penguin colonies and lava rocks of Punta Moreno, as well as the saltwater Darwin Lake located inside of a volcanic crater at Caleta Tagus.

Ecuadorian-owned, family-run expedition line Quasar operates 8-day and 15-day safari-style itineraries that focus on facilitating meaningful wildlife encounters for the small group of guests on board. With these immersive sailings, you might be swimming with sea turtles one day and cruising on a Zodiac boat amid a pod of dolphins the next. The line’s two yachts are designed for intimate trips, carrying a maximum of 32 guests. The 16-passenger Grace yacht has an especially intriguing history: Grace Kelly, who used it for her honeymoon in 1956, and has since been carefully restored to its original opulent glory. Guests can even stay in the revamped Grace Kelly suite, where the iconic actress spent her two-week honeymoon. Both yachts offer modern amenities like oversized hot tubs, al-fresco bars and lounges, sun decks, and more. Everything from meals to shore excursions to the open bar is included in the cruise fare.

Guests also have onboard access to kayaks, paddle boards, and snorkeling equipment for interacting directly with marine life like reef sharks, sea lions, and marine iguanas whenever the mood strikes. With such a small group, tours are immersive and personalized. Travelers can expect daily Zodiac landings across remote sites on islands like Espanola, Genovesa, Fernandina, Isabela, and Bartolome with expert naturalist guides.

While Flora can fit up to 100 passengers on board, excursions are limited to groups of 12 guests or fewer.

Sailing aboard the purpose-built ship Celebrity Flora strikes a perfect balance between relaxing on a luxurious floating resort and chasing the thrill of an adventurous expedition. The all-suite, all-veranda ship offers each guest a personal suite attendant, menus curated by a Michelin-starred chef, and an all-inclusive policy that covers drinks, meals, shore excursions, and even flights. Travelers can also expect a personal touch from crew, with 100 passengers on board and excursions that are limited to groups of 12 guests or fewer. Tours included memorable experiences like walks through lava tunnels, panga boat rides along rocky shorelines teeming with Galapagos penguins and sea lions, guided hikes to see blue-footed boobies, frigate birds, giant tortoises, rare flora, and ancient cacti.

Opportunities to spot diverse wildlife don’t end once travelers return to the ship. Celebrity Flora is outfitted with Sky Suites featuring the line’s signature Infinite Veranda that brings the extraordinary outdoor surroundings directly into your room. The window transforms into an open-air veranda at the touch of a button, allowing travelers to fully immerse themselves in the wondrous landscapes without even leaving their room. Plus, features like solar panels, reverse-osmosis water filtration, and dynamic positioning are gentle on the islands’ precious resources.

How early should I book a Galapagos cruise?

For the widest selection of vessels and sailing dates, aim to book your cruise four to nine months ahead of your intended sailing. More spontaneous travelers may find last-minute deals booking two to eight weeks ahead of their intended departure, though some itineraries will be sold out by then.

Getting to the Galapagos requires some logistical planning. After flying into Quito or Guayaquil, passengers typically spend a night in one of these mainland destinations before flying to the islands to board their ships. Your cruise line will tell you where to be on the islands for your departure, and in some cases, flights from the mainland will be included (or booked for an additional fee).

When is the best time to cruise the Galapagos Islands?

With a consistently mild climate year-round, the Galapagos can be visited at any time, although certain seasons offer exceptional wildlife viewing. December is when the giant tortoises hatch, and July marks the mating season for blue-footed boobies and short-eared owls. In April and May, marine iguanas typically hatch, while sea turtles begin laying their eggs at the start of the year. Given the diverse wildlife and year-round natural phenomena, there's never a "wrong" time to visit the islands.

The Galapagos Islands aren’t a bargain destination. Expect to pay somewhere between $5,000 and $12,000 per traveler, depending on the ship, itinerary, and length of the voyage, though there are options starting in the $3,000s.

What kind of wildlife can I expect to see on a Galapagos cruise?

The Galapagos Islands are renowned for their unique wildlife, including giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, and sea lions. The islands’ ecosystems are so diverse that you can see a variety of species in different environments, from volcanic shores to lush highlands.

This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Paris Wilson.

#6156. The Best Places to Go in Asia in 2027

It’s that time of year when we drop our expert-curated list of the best places to go in Asia in 2027. But before we do, we have to acknowledge that 2026 was a challenging year across the continent. Amid a shifting geopolitical environment and climate change events, there is now a renewed sense of purpose as communities across Asia look at art, food, and nature for a brighter 2027.

Our list of the best places to go in Asia in 2027 showcases the sheer diversity of experiences on offer for every kind of traveler. For the outdoorsy, new long distance hiking trails in the Caucasus, via ancient wine caves and Silk Road-era caravansaries, take you deep into Armenia’s history. Tourists will always flock to Japan’s glittering megacities, but on their outskirts—like in Niigata Prefecture just two hours from Tokyo—regenerative tourism models like the Echigo-Tsumari Art Triennale draw visitors into the country’s stunning rural landscapes.

Penang is a foodie favorite, and 2027 brings a clutch of revamped stays and inventive new restaurants spotlighting heritage ingredients. Further afield in the Philippines, the emerging slow-food culture in Negros Occidental is worth planning a trip around.

For that vibrant city energy, 2027 is a big year, as Jaipur celebrates its 300th anniversary with a year-round calendar of commemorative events. Bangkok has a whole roster of buzzy new hotel openings lined up, while Shanghai is set to see a culture-filled year with the biennale and new museums along the waterfront. From skyscraper-dotted metropolises to remote landscapes sustained by community initiatives, Asia gives everyone a reason to visit in 2027. —Malavika Bhattacharya

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: nature, history, and slow travel on foot

Amernia's Transcaucasian Trail is dotted with monasteries, ancient caves, and roadside inns—and in 2027, it will feel even easier to tackle thanks to new maps, updated trail sections, and trekking services.

Built among the peaks and valleys of the Caucasus, Armenia’s ancient roots and mountainous landscapes reward slow travel. Along the country’s two long-distance trails, the Armenian National Trail (ANT) and the Transcaucasian Trail (TCT), medieval monasteries rise above dramatic gorges, Silk Road-era caravansaries dot historic mountain routes, and ancient caves recall thousands of years of winemaking history. In Yerevan, one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, historic fortresses and pale pink stone buildings sit side by side with a colorful café and restaurant scene.

In 2027, Armenia's growing outdoor scene makes it especially exciting for adventurous travelers. The TCT, which will eventually span nearly 1,900 miles across Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan, is becoming easier to tackle with new downloadable maps, updated trail sections and signage, and trekking services offering itinerary planning and luggage transfers. The Armenian section of the TCT extends from Arevik National Park in the south, past Syunik’s cave dwellings and the Tatev Monastery, rising against deep river gorges; through the volcanic massifs of the Gegham Mountains, the forests of Dilijan National Park, and ending at Lake Arpi National Park near Georgia.

Meanwhile, the ANT, a 620-mile network that will eventually connect more than 100 villages, opened its first sections in June 2026 with more to open next year. Trails currently extend through Tavush and Lori, and soon Vayots Dzor, where visitors can birdwatch in alpine steppes, stay with families, and cook herb-filled meals with local hosts, while sampling lavash (Armenia's UNESCO-listed flatbread) baked in a deep, clay oven, and regional bounties like forest berries, mushrooms, cornelian cherry, and rosehip soup. Collectively, the trails offer a new way to experience Armenia's landscapes and communities on foot. —Alicia Erickson

Go for: a luxury and lifestyle hotel boom reshaping the city

Golden hour in Bangkok Yai's historic canal district, beneath the towering Wat Paknam Big Buddha, showcases the bustling city's eternal allure.

Already one of the world’s most-visited cities, Bangkok is giving travelers new reasons to return in 2027. A remarkable wave of hotel openings is part of a broader luxury boom sweeping the Thai capital, which ranked fourth globally for new luxury store openings in 2025. There’s been a recent influx of designer flagships, including Gucci's renovated and reopened boutique, Ralph Lauren’s concept store at Central Embassy, and Acne Studios at Siam Paragon.

Bangkok is also expanding its world-class dining, contemporary art, and urban green spaces, while preserving the street stalls, markets, and neighborhood restaurants that made it famous. It now has nine restaurants on Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants list, more than any other city in the region, with acclaimed newcomers, such as the reopening of Sra Bua by Num Weerawat at Siam Kempinski Hotel Bangkok, and a growing natural wine scene.

The city’s hotel boom spans luxury, lifestyle, and design. Canopy by Hilton Bangkok Sukhumvit opened in August 2026, while Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit; The Langham, Custom House, Bangkok; and YOTEL Bangkok Sukhumvit are accepting reservations for later in the year. Other 2027 openings include Conrad Bangkok Sukhumvit Queen's Park, the renowned Siam Motors Building, which is transforming into the Siam Pan Pacific Bangkok, Pan Pacific Serviced Suites Bangkok, and Hotel Indigo by IHG. There have also been rumblings that Belmond’s luxury Eastern and Oriental Express will return to Bangkok in 2027.

The Green Bangkok 2030 Project—an urban plan to increase Bangkok's green spaces to 110 square feet per person—helped drive the 2026 reopening of the mile-long Green Bridge, a car-free greenway connecting Lumpini Park and Benjakitti Park. Song Wat Road has emerged as a modern cultural hub—with famed street food, an array of art spaces, artisan coffee shops, and vintage clothing—amid expanded plans to transform Chinatown.

The December 2025 opening of Dib Bangkok, Thailand’s first museum devoted exclusively to international contemporary art, was another significant milestone. Australia’s Museum of Old and New Art has also announced plans for a Bangkok outpost, further strengthening the city’s reputation as a serious art destination. —Kaila Yu

Go for: the Pink City’s 300th anniversary

Old becomes new in Jaipur, which celebrates its 300th year as a city in 2027. The opulent Sarvato Jaipur (pictured), for example, was once a terrace pavilion used for an audience with the maharaja.

In 1727, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II established Jaipur as the capital of his kingdom, envisioning it as a financial and artistic hub. As the city marks its 300th year in 2027, the City Palace—the current residence of the erstwhile royals—readies for the occasion with new exhibits across its galleries, as well as in private spaces not usually accessible to the public. Traces of Us, an exhibit by the Jaipur Centre for Art, marks the anniversary with contemporary works by artists like M.F. Husain and Bharti Kher displayed across the palace. A terrace pavilion once used for an audience with the maharaja is now the stylish, open-air restaurant the Sarvato, where Sawai Padmanabh Singh partners with hotelier Abhishek Honawar to showcase a modern, six-course menu championing both the everyday and the celebratory food of Rajasthan, served with a spectacular view of Jaipur.

Honawar, best known for his boutique Michelin Key property the Johri, a restored 19th-century haveli in the Old City, added three more suites this year to the hotel’s original five keys. Set to open later in 2026 is Hawa Haveli, an eight-key stay with a restaurant and cocktail bar, housed in a 19th-century merchant mansion—another intimate boutique property from the same team.

For three days in December 2026, the Jaigarh Heritage Festival brings folk artists and craftspeople to the 11th-century Jaigarh Fort to celebrate the city’s 300th anniversary, while the Jaipur Literature Festival in January brings the stalwarts of the literary world to the Pink City.

A themed walk, Jaipur 300: A City of Craft and Courtyards, led by Neeraj Chauhan of Jaipurnama, traces three centuries of living heritage. And to carry a piece of Jaipur back with you, the Jaipur Watch Company has released two special timepieces inspired by the City Palace’s beautiful Leheriya Gate and Peacock Gate. —Shalbha Sarda

Go for: slow food culture, heritage ingredients, and eco-friendly experiences

The 18-villa Manami Resort in Sipalay offers a conservation-first stay that connects visitors to the surrounding landscape.

Cooking at fish farm 7 Hectares, which uses hyperlocal ingredients, is a way to tap into Negros Occidental's slow-food movement.

Formerly home to wealthy sugar barons and sprawling plantations, the 19th-century beginnings of industrialized sugar production, today Negros Occidental is at the heart of a thriving slow-food scene. In 2027, this Negros Island province, 330 miles south of the Philippines capital Manila, will play host to the prestigious triennial Organic World Congress, as well as the returning Terra Madre Asia and Pacific slow-food festival.

In the biennale’s first iteration, Michelin-starred chefs appeared alongside local producers like Francisco “Kiko” Torno, owner of 7 Hectares fish farm, whose pop-up kitchen serves slow-food dishes cooked with hyperlocal ingredients. And he’s not the only one: The island’s farmers, fishermen, cooks, and chefs are all determined to champion the homegrown, and many welcome visitors on local food tours.

A short boat ride off the coast takes nature lovers to the award-winning Suyac Island Mangrove Eco-Park, which is expected to be nominated for the prestigious ASEAN Sustainable Community-Based Tourism Award in 2027. Islanders guide visitors through an old mangrove forest with giant fruit bats, navigated by wooden walkways, telling stories about their community. Stay at conservation-first Manami Resort in Sipalay, which joined the Michelin hotels list in May 2026, and has 18 villas, each with its own “nature butler,” and a marine biologist to help guests to tune into their environment. —Claire Turrell

Go for: landscapes reimagined through art

The Hoshitoge terraced rice fields, fed by Niigata’s winter snowmelt, still yield an abundant harvest each autumn. It is here, in these zones between human settlements and mountain landscapes—known as satoyama in Japanese—that Niigata's beauty shines.

Travel in Japan is no longer just about the big cities. For travelers interested in sustainable tourism, the focus is shifting to rural areas, such as Niigata Prefecture on Japan’s west coast, just two hours from Tokyo. In Japan, “satoyama” describes the transition zones between human settlements (sato) and mountain landscapes (yama), where communities have traditionally managed forests and farmland in harmony with nature. As rural populations decline, these cultural landscapes are disappearing, but in Niigata, the Echigo-Tsumari Art Triennale has emerged as a model for regenerative tourism. Returning for its 10th edition in July 2027, the contemporary art festival uses creativity to revive the region.

Spanning Tokamachi and Tsunan in southern Niigata, Echigo-Tsumari is a vast landscape of rice terraces, forests, and villages. The triennale brings large-scale works by Japanese and international artists into abandoned buildings and open spaces—from MAD Architects’ immersive Tunnel of Light in Kiyotsu Gorge to Christian Boltanski’s meditative The Last Class inside a shuttered school—while bringing revenue to depopulated villages. Locals are involved as guides and hosts, ensuring income stays within the community.

At a time when overtourism is challenging Japan’s hotspots, the festival demonstrates how cultural tourism can support rural communities off the beaten track. This ethos extends to Niigata’s hospitality scene. In June 2026, NIPPONIA Niigata Furumachi Hanamachi transformed three historic buildings in Niigata City’s geisha district into a dispersed hotel. Guests are encouraged to treat the entire neighborhood as the hotel and take part in cultural experiences such as geisha performances. Yadoya Dōmichi, a similar dispersed-hotel concept in the mountains outside Itoigawa that accepts just one group per night, opened in January 2026 and offers guests the chance to join in with everyday village activities such as planting rice in spring and building snow huts in winter. —Karen Gardiner

Go for: new ways to explore the island’s cultural and culinary heritage

Root House by Gēn is one of several Penang restaurants embracing the city's culinary roots anew.

Soori Penang, a shophouse-turned-hotel, is a star example of how the city's historic buildings have been given a second life.

Penang’s kopitiams, hawker centers, and beloved nasi kandar joints culminate in a layered culinary landscape which, like its styles of architecture and sites of worship, reflects over two centuries worth of maritime trade, British colonialism, and waves of settlers from China, India, and beyond. Now, a clutch of chefs are spinning modern takes on heritage produce. At newcomer Root House by Gēn, chef-founder Johnson Wong interprets the movement of people from China to Malaysia into a menu that presents traditional ingredients like century egg and fermented bean curd in a fine-dining format.

Within the mural-lined streets of George Town, historic shophouses-turned-hotels offer firsthand immersion into the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Newcomer Soori Penang is noteworthy as it was driven by a deeply personal restoration mission: Architect Soo K. Chan once called the now-converted shophouses home. Part of the Leading Hotels of the World, it resides alongside the 175-year-old Khoo Kongsi clan house and will soon unveil the three-bedroom Clan House Suite as well as a cigar and whiskey lounge. The Qing Suites, meanwhile, is a forgotten 1904 annex within the Cheong Fatt Tze or The Blue Mansion of Crazy Rich Asians fame. Once housing the servants’ quarters, it now stands as a 13-suite boutique property on the historic Lebuh Leith.

A brainchild of Hong Kong actress Amy Yip, Penang’s affinity for durian will translate to the world’s first durian-themed luxury hotel, complete with private tasting lounge, expected to debut in late 2027.

In early 2027, the popular Gurney Drive Hawker Center will relocate to Gurney Bay, an expansive promenade and public park facing the Andaman Sea. Further afield, a new cable car at Penang Hill, a UNESCO-designated biosphere reserve, will both serve as an additional tourist attraction and alleviate the strain on the century-old funicular that ascends to its peak, 2,700 feet above sea level. Operations are set to begin in late 2027. —Samia Qaiyum

Go for: a tropical island transforming ahead of the global spotlight

The wellness-focused Regent Phú Quốc shows how this destination has become one of Southeast Asia's fastest growing resort hubs—and 2027 is the year to reap the benefits for yourself.

Phú Quốc has transformed over the past decade from a sleepy fishing island into one of Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing resort hubs. White-sand beaches and fishing villages still edge an interior blanketed by protected rainforest parks, but increasingly share space with resorts and entertainment complexes. Now, another transformation is underway as the island prepares to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November 2027.

The scale alone is dramatic: SOM is designing a waterfront district with an 800,000-square-foot convention center and performance arena. Phú Quốc International Airport is expanding toward a capacity of 24 million passengers annually, while homegrown Sun PhuQuoc Airways builds connections across Asia. Thousands of hotel rooms are coming, too, with Rixos, the Luxury Collection, JW Marriott Marquis, Moxy, and Conrad among some of the many openings slated over the next year.

For all the development, there are still quieter corners—whether kayaking mangrove-lined waterways in the north or checking into the pleasantly understated, wellness-centric Regent Phu Quoc. But this is also a place to surrender to spectacle: soar over turquoise waters on an 6-mile cable car or catch the nightly extravaganza of lasers, acrobatics, and pyrotechnics at the Kiss of the Sea show. —Dan Q. Dao

Go for: a revitalized waterfront best explored on foot

Snøhetta's Shanghai Grand Opera House venue and landmark, which opened in October 2026, illustrates the cultural revolution stirring within the city.

China’s trading powerhouse, Shanghai, sits on the Huangpu River, a commercial lifeline dividing the city, and home to its most famous waterside promenade, the Bund. South along the river, the 16th Shanghai Biennale will open in November 2027 at the Power Station of Art, a contemporary art museum crowned with a 540-foot chimney.

In the West Bund, a former industrial waterfront turned arts district, where more museums are joining its riverside row, the annual West Bund Art and Design fair will draw galleries from across Asia and beyond in the same weeks.

On the river’s opposite shore, in Houtan, Snøhetta's Shanghai Grand Opera House opened in October 2026. It’s a world-class venue for the performing arts and a civic landmark in its own right: a spiraling ramp climbs the fan-shaped roof to a terrace open to all, with Expo Culture Park spread out below.

Shanghai’s hotel landscape is also shifting in 2027. Fairmont Peace Hotel, Victor Sassoon’s art deco creation, and Bund landmark dating to 1929, which once welcomed film star Charlie Chaplin and playwright Noël Coward, is due to reopen as Raffles Peace Hotel Shanghai, with its “historic treasures” preserved. And on the North Bund, a disused office block facing the Bund across the water becomes Lux's first Shanghai hotel, Lux On the Bund, with 100 river-view rooms. —Yolaine Feng

Go for: a regional food and wine scene, with ancient landscapes and new hotels

To appreciate Yunnan in 2027, pair the buzzy city energy of Kunming, which has turned into a destination in its own right, with serene countrysides accessible via towns like Lijiang, where the Amandayan (pictured) is based.

China, as it appears on our TikTok and Instagram feeds, is all gleaming skyscrapers, driverless cars, and neon-lit megacities. Yunnan, in China’s southwest, offers another view: a part of the country where those same advances exist alongside snowcapped mountains, ancient tea forests, highland lakes, and villages tucked into valleys. Start in Kunming, the provincial capital. Long regarded as a gateway to the rest of Yunnan, the city has become a destination in its own right. Here in Spring City a few experiences are essential, like digging into crossing-the-bridge noodles (guòqiáo mǐxiàn) and wandering the Dounan flower market, one of the largest in Asia. There are also new restaurants and bars giving the city fresh energy—and many of which have Yunnan wine now appearing on their menus (Shangri-La’s high-altitude wines, in particular, are starting to make a name for themselves in China). For a taste of the new, book a table at Yijin Sting or Cui House, both of which pair contemporary Yunnanese cooking with local pours. Between meals, the new Cuihu Urban Greenway, opened in 2025, makes it easier to explore the city center on foot; it connects Cuihu Lake with Kunming Old Street, which boasts museums, cafés, and historic façades. The hotel scene is kicking up too: Shangri-La Kunming opened in 2026 with an immersive local tea experience.

Kunming is just the starting point. From there, head west to the city of Dali, where the Cangshan mountains rise behind the old city and Erhai Lake stretches out beyond it. The Three Pagodas have stood at the foot of the mountains for more than a thousand years. Mostly, though, Dali is a place to slow down—and the Dali Edition hotel, opened in June 2026, caters to travelers who wish to do so.

Further flung are destinations like Lijiang, with a charming Old Town and easy access to the scenic Blue Moon Valley. Between Lijiang and Shangri-La lies Tiger Leaping Gorge, where the Jinsha River squeezes between the over-three-mile-high mountains, where one- and two-day treks are well worth the effort. Shangri-La, at the northern end of the trip, is largely Tibetan in culture: Time your visit to Songzanlin Monastery for the morning chants, then spend a late afternoon in Dukezong Ancient Town before walking up the hill to the giant prayer wheel, where you can join locals in spinning it. Yunnan promises much to explore—and rewards those willing to dig deep into its reaches. —Ali Farooqui

#6155. American Unveils Limited-Edition Jacket Made of Recycled Aircraft Seats

American Airlines is joining in the “Cyber Week” shopping holiday with the planned release of a branded jacket made from reclaimed leather from the carrier’s old aircraft, including the McDonnell Douglas MD-80.

The special, limited-edition MA-1 flight jackets are made by Alpha Industries and come with an American patch celebrating the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

The airline plans to make 10 jackets available for purchase each day from Nov. 30 through Dec. 4, at the price of 200,000 AAdvantage miles each.

Alpha Industries said it received 650 seats from American for the project. Each jacket requires 10 to 12 seats to make, depending on the quality of the material.

American is also advertising its other branded merchandise ahead of the holidays, including suitcases and limited-edition pickleball paddles made in collaboration with Volair.

From Nov. 27 through Dec. 2, AAdvantage members can save up to 50% when purchasing 500,000 or more miles.

#6154. Ryanair Delays Free Seat Assignments, Says Passengers Who Don’t Pay “Clearly Don’t Mind Where They Sit”

Ryanair passengers who decline to pay for seat selection must now wait until only a few hours before departure to learn where they will sit. The airline says the change preserves more choice for customers willing to pay, which makes commercial sense. It also creates another incentive to purchase a seat simply to end the uncertainty.

Ryanair has changed when it assigns complimentary random seats to passengers who do not purchase one.

Previously, passengers generally received their seat assignment when checking in up to 24 hours before departure. Under the new approach, the seat may not appear on the digital boarding pass until approximately three to four hours before the flight.

The change was introduced with Ryanair’s winter schedule at the end of October.

Passengers can still check in beginning 72 hours before departure, but those who decline to pay for a seat may have to wait until the day of travel for the airline to update their boarding pass with an actual seat assignment.

Ryanair told RTE that it received complaints from passengers who wanted to purchase a particular seat on the day of departure, only to find that desirable seats had already been distributed through free random allocation.

Its explanation included a very Ryanair-like observation:

“Passengers who choose a free of charge random seat clearly don’t mind where they sit.”

Therefore, Ryanair now keeps more seats available for purchase until closer to departure. Passengers who have selected random seating will have their digital boarding passes automatically updated once the airline assigns them a seat.

The logic is understandable: if someone is willing to pay for an aisle or window seat three hours before departure, Ryanair would rather sell it than discover it gave that seat away for free the previous evening. But let’s not pretend that preserving customer choice is the only objective here…those who are going to buy a seat usually do so in advance, so we are only talking about last-minute purchases.

I have no problem with Ryanair charging for advance seat assignments. That is the low-cost carrier “unbundled” model: advertise a very inexpensive base fare and allow passengers to decide which extras are worth purchasing.

I have flown Ryanair many times and approach it with those expectations. If I care where I sit, I pay. If I do not, I take whatever the airline gives me (of course hoping I end up with a window or aisle seat).

But the timing of this change creates pressure that did not exist before. A passenger can complete check-in yet remain uncertain about the seat assignment until shortly before leaving for the airport. Some will become impatient or anxious and pay simply to resolve it.

That is certainly good ancillary-revenue strategy. It is also another example of Ryanair understanding exactly how to monetize uncertainty. The airline knows that passengers become increasingly willing to spend as departure approaches. A middle seat may be tolerable when the trip is weeks away, but somehow looks much less appealing on the morning of the flight.

Ryanair’s family seating policy remains important here.

Under the airline’s published policy, children between two and 11 years old must be seated beside at least one accompanying adult. The adult is required to reserve a seat, while up to four children receive adjacent reserved seats without an additional seat-selection charge. Additional adults and passengers aged 12 or older who do not purchase seats may be assigned elsewhere.

Families should be aware that they are not guaranteed to be seated next to eachother (and it would not surprise me if the Ryanair algorithm specially avoids this in order to encourage famlies to pre-pay for seats on the next trip).

Ryanair now waits until approximately three to four hours before departure to assign complimentary random seats, allowing it to preserve more desirable inventory for passengers willing to pay.

The commercial reasoning is clear, and I do not fault Ryanair for selling seat assignments. But delaying the free assignment also creates anxiety that will persuade some passengers to purchase a seat they otherwise would not have bought. It is clever revenue management, but hardly an improvement for passengers.

And while we are on the topic of Ryanair, can I just say how much I loved this tweet:

#6153. Cayman Airways Adds New Route to U.S.

Cayman Airways will launch a new seasonal service to the U.S. next year.

Starting May 21, 2027, the carrier will connect Grand Cayman and Nashville, Tennessee. Flights will operate twice per week, on Mondays and Fridays, through Aug. 16.

Tickets will become available for purchase early next month, officials said.

Cayman Airways is the flag carrier of the Cayman Islands and has its main hub at Owen Roberts International Airport in Grand Cayman.

Its current U.S. destinations are Miami, Tampa, Florida, Austin, Texas, Denver, and Los Angeles.

#6152. BermudAir Adds 10 New Destinations, 18 New Routes

Bermudian flag carrier BermudAir will nearly double its U.S. footprint next year as it launches new connections across North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The carrier announced Tuesday that it will serve New Orleans; Nashville, Tennessee; New Haven, Connecticut; Burlington, Vermont; Portland, Maine; San Antonio; New Brunswick, Canada; Ocho Rios, Jamaica; San Salvador, El Salvador; and San Pedro Sula, Honduras, for the first time.

Accompanying the 10 new destinations are 18 new routes. BermudAir is also moving to expand service to existing markets, such as Bermuda, Anguilla, Belize, Grand Cayman, Guatemala, and Turks and Caicos.

“From New Orleans and Nashville to San Antonio and New England, we’re seeing tremendous interest in what BermudAir offers,” founder and CEO Adam Scott said in a news release.

BermudAir currently serves eight U.S. cities, all on or close to the East Coast, and three destinations in Canada. Its main hub is L.F. Wade International Airport in St. George’s, Bermuda.

#6151. On a Ranch in Wyoming, a Stressed-Out Editor Gets in Sync With a Lazy Horse

I used to avoid horses the same way I’d avoid palm readers. While my friends chased $5 readings in Downtown Manhattan, I preferred to keep the velvet curtain closed.

I was convinced that once a fortune teller held my hands in hers, she would trace a life line abruptly cut short or reveal a heart line splintered beyond repair. So I’d sit on the stoop, hands safely secured in the pockets of my jacket. Horses and psychics, I believed, shared the same dark, all-knowing eyes.

The 80,000-acre ranch is nestled between Wyoming's Bighorn Mountains and Paintrock Canyon.

The first time I rode a horse was 10 years ago in Costa Rica, my body clenched for the entirety of the 20-minute sunset beach stroll. “They can sense your fear,” I remember the guide telling me. “Just try to relax.”

Over the next decade I’d continue to receive similar advice—from my mother in a well-intentioned effort to soothe her overthinking eldest daughter, but also from doctors and massage therapists and boyfriends. I am trying, I would say. There was nothing effortless about me, and that was the problem.

So when I found out on the plane to Wyoming that the camp at Ranchlands I was headed to—an 80,000-acre ranch nestled between the Bighorn Mountains and Paintrock Canyon—would have no Wi-Fi, cell service, or nary an outlet to plug into, I sent out panicked slacks and emails apologizing. They tell me there is a hill with a few bars, I tell my manager. I will find it.

The guest accommodations at Paintrock Canyon Ranch

This may come as a surprise, but like most creatives who have converted their personal passions into paychecks, travel editors are sneaky workaholics, adept at turning vacations into deliverables. At customs checkpoints, I’ll still catch myself stumbling when asked if I’m traveling for business or leisure. When the world is your office, is the answer: both? Or neither?

The answer was particularly murky this time around, as I was traveling to Ranchlands for a writing and riding retreat hosted by author Molly Wizenberg. I’d be joined by nine other solo women travelers; labor lawyers, criminologists, educators, and Fortune 500 marketers who I imagined also struggled to relax. After all, their idea of a vacation was to ride five hours a day and sleep in a tent (albeit elegant), all whilst working on novels and memoirs in between.

We introduce ourselves while seated at a long wooden picnic table overlooking a gurgling creek, into which I will plunge each afternoon to wash off the desert dust. All around us, towering limestone walls encircle the camp, a gently sloping field of shin-high sagebrush. Contrasted against the layered prairie grasses, the opaque form and sharp lines of the white canvas tents remind me of a famous painting, but I’m not sure which one. There is something archetypal about this place, and it leaves me with a lingering sense of dejá vu, as if I was remembering a long-forgotten dream.

From the main camp, guests can go hiking, fly fishing, and horseback riding.

Over the next five days, Molly tells us, we will split our time between horseback riding through the surrounding high desert and mountainous terrain and group writing workshops. For the entirety of the trip, each of us will be paired with a horse, a match based on stated riding experience. (Or, your deepest hopes and fears, should you have disclosed these in the pre-arrival form.)

The first time I meet my horse, I’m overwhelmed with the nerves of a blind date. When a cowboy making horseshoe repairs offers me a cigarette, I almost take him up on it. “This is José,” Oliver, an Australian wrangler with a charming snaggletooth grin, tells me as he adjusts the saddle. “He’s a bit lazy, this one.”

As I reach up to pet his coarse black mane, I wait for José to flinch away from my touch, his flaring nostrils surely sniffing out my incompetence. With a horse, there’s no pretending, and no amount of Westernwear could hide my East Coast Puritan roots. While some of my ancestors had made it as far as California, for the most part they sailed across and stayed. Such pioneering ambitions as Manifest Destiny were nowhere to be found in my family tree.

But José doesn't look through me, he just looks at me. And if he does see into the depths of my spur-bearing soul, he doesn’t seem bothered by it. When I climb atop the saddle, he shows no signs of wanting to move. I look down at his long eyelashes, fluttering gently. That's okay, I think to myself. I'm not a morning person either.

“You two are a good match,” says Ella, our wrangler and guide, as the group rides single-file beneath what the ranchers call The Red Wall, an ancient red rock mesa that gives way to sprawling desert. It takes nearly two hours to cross the dusty valley, its rust-colored dirt baking in the sun—it's as though we are climbing out of a shallow clay bowl painted with pastel pigment, waiting to be brought to the kiln.

Our daily rides are approximately five hours long, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., though some are shorter. Lunch—which one afternoon included melt-in-your-mouth pork belly and a quinoa salad—is eaten out in the field with the horses, who happily accept the remains of any apple rinds. A short writing exercise follows, and sometimes a cowgirl nap, our backs leaning up against a tree trunk or laying down flat in the tall grasses, hat brims tilted over our eyes. Dinner—fresh fish, meat, and vegetables prepared over an open-fire kitchen—is enjoyed creekside back at camp beneath twinkle lights. By the end of each day, I’m so tired that I fall asleep at 9 p.m. and before the sun has fully set, despite promising myself I’d stay up late enough to see the stars.

Most of the cooking is done over open fire, using local ingredients (including beef from the ranch).

Breakfasts and dinners are communal meals, while lunch is packed and eaten out in the field.

One morning on the trail, the group turns to the topic of AI, and how to make sense of it in a place like this. Our brains, we all agree, feel healthier without the constant distractions of our phones. During the writing workshops interspersed throughout the day, most of us opt to write by hand. My thoughts are clearer, less muddled. There are no extra tabs to open—no research rabbit holes or thesaurus queries to get lost in.

At the beginning of the retreat, Molly asks us each to share one sentence on what writing represents to us. I think of answering “my job,” but instead I say “it’s how I think”—a response that two others echo. Another woman answers, “writing is hard.” We all laugh in agreement, and I wonder why we torture ourselves in this way. Especially now, with the temptation of automation hovering over every email draft and browser.

The bulk of our writing is done in the afternoons, when we bring our notebooks and pens to the “lounge” tent and settle into couches and cowhide chairs to discuss the previous day’s readings before tackling a writing prompt. It’s a welcome break for our shaky thighs and sore tuchuses—and a satisfying tiredness I find myself looking forward to.

Tapas, drinks, and mocktails are served creekside.

Our only assignment for the week? “To Be Absolutely Yourself.” The retreat's title, as Molly explains, means exploring our strangest and most personal obsessions, irrational fears, and inexplicable crushes, with the idea that these idiosyncrasies—such as Sam Anderson’s secret mole that he convinced himself was cancerous for almost a decade—are our most universal experiences. Though some in the group are working on pieces they hope to publish one day, we are reminded on multiple occasions to write without thinking about the end result: not what the poem or essay might turn into, or whether anyone would want to read it. It’s a way of writing that someone who speaks the language of commissioning rates and word counts rarely gets to practice. What is my writing when it’s not a product? I jot down. What is work without a job?

Midway through the week, a smaller group of us embark on an optional ride up into the canyon, weaving between the anemone-like skeletons of burnt juniper trees, sunlight transforming the deep grey charcoal into shimmering shades of silver. José slowly trudges forward, dodging stumps and rocks with careful, decisive footing. Like people, I learn that horses may be better suited for different jobs in line with their personality; some enjoy herding cattle and others are more suited to trail riding. Others, like José, are happiest chewing grass in a meadow.

José is in no rush to get to where we are going, and in accepting that, my thoughts slow down to match his meditative pace. I am not sure if I would be able to sink into this relaxed state if I didn’t have somewhere else to direct my focus: my hands on the reins, the directions transmitted with a quick squeeze of my thighs, and my balance as we climb higher up the canyon wall.

Ranchlands' cattle business uses conservation-focused cattle management

It is counterintuitive to try and go and learn a new skill when you are burned out—but I was coming to realize that sometimes, relaxation takes work. That we write because it is hard, not in spite of it. In an environment like this one, these facts feel obviously simple. But I also know how easy they will be to forget, when the distractions return.

Perhaps that’s why so much of modern travel is now packaged as a retreat. The travel industry, my publication included, has been busy finding new names for this widespread desire toward a similar desire to unplug and reconnect with the physical world: skillcations, dead-zone retreats, analogue travel, cowboy-core, and a growing list of other buzzy trends.

In this way, ranch life has once again emerged as an American frontier. As one guest writes on the Ranchlands’ website testimonial page: “As a professional working in the corporate world, my stay at Ranchlands allowed me to step away from all of the noise in the chaos that is always coming at me. It felt like a reset for my nervous system and the most restful time that I have had in a long time.” Signed, Larissa M.

On our final ride, our wrangler Ella, who grew up working on her mother’s equine therapy farm in North Carolina, explains that the heart of a horse is nine times the size of a human’s, creating an electromagnetic field that pulses with and around that of its rider—which can form a symbiotic relationship between horse and rider that can even lead your heart rates to sync up. Though horses are often associated with bravery and courage, in reality many are quite skittish and easily spooked, by butterflies and birds and the wind and plastic irrigation piping. The same way a horse can calm down an anxious rider, a strong rider can give a nervous horse confidence.

When we turn back toward the ranch José picks up the pace to pass the group, uncharacteristically leading the charge. “He’s a bit sad today,” Oliver tells me. “We left his girlfriend back at the barn.” Her name, he says, is Pistol.

How did I not realize it sooner? The drifting attention, the constant daydreaming, the sudden burst of energy when it was time to go home. José was not a lazy horse, I realized. He was a boy with a big heart and a relaxed nervous system. And he was in love.

Ranchlands' five-night vacations start from $4,150 per person, including accommodation, meals, and activities (closed from mid-October to mid-May).

#6150. Lufthansa Turns Airplane Etiquette Into Clothing

Lufthansa is turning airplane etiquette into a clothing collection, including a new shirt reminding passengers that there is no need to stand up immediately after landing. I like the idea and agree with much of the advice, though standing up is not necessarily the problem…pushing past everyone else is.

Lufthansa has announced that four items from its Travel Etiquette Collection will go on sale through the WorldShop beginning November 27, 2026.

The collection debuted in August and was not originally intended for sale. Lufthansa says the response prompted a retail edition, including a new shirt based on the most popular suggestion from its social media community.

Each design is limited to 250 individually numbered pieces. Lufthansa will donate its licensing proceeds to help alliance, the Lufthansa Group’s aid organization (that is the licensing revenue, rather than necessarily the entire purchase price).

Prices were not included in the announcement.

First off, I love these…simple yet stylish.

As to the messaging itself, I understand why the shirt appeals to people. We have all watched passengers spring up as though standing in the aisle will somehow make the jet bridge attach faster.

And if the aircraft is still moving or the seatbelt sign remains illuminated, it should go without saying that you stay seated.

But once the aircraft is parked and passengers are permitted to get up, I have no objection to someone standing. After several hours in an economy class seat, stretching your legs is perfectly understandable. An aisle passenger can also retrieve a bag and be ready to leave when the rows ahead have cleared.

The problem is the person who charges forward from row 28 and wedges himself beside row 19, apparently convinced that everyone else is sitting there for his convenience.

Stand if you want. Just wait your turn to leave.

(The only exception I would make are the circumstances in which the crew asks passengers to remain seated so travelers with tight connections can get off first. That requires everyone to cooperate, including those of us who might otherwise prefer to stand…but I also have a problem with the “free riders” in those situations…another issue for another day.)

My favorite in this collection is the “Recline Responsibly” message, which strikes me as common sense, but something so many passengers are so rude about.

If an airline installs a reclining seat, passengers should generally be able to use that feature. But look behind you first and recline slowly. Giving the person behind you a moment to adjust a laptop or move a drink costs you very little.

During meal service, the seat should be upright, but other than that, recline away…just gently.

We spend so much time arguing about whether reclining is acceptable that we sometimes overlook how much the manner of doing it matters. A slow adjustment is very different from throwing your seat back without warning.

Lufthansa will begin selling four limited-edition etiquette items on November 27. I like the collection, particularly the reminder to recline responsibly. But I can’t say I’ll be up late waiting to buy it…how about you?

#6148. “We Have Had Alien Sightings Out There” ATC Tells American Eagle Pilot After Unexplained Traffic Alert

An American Eagle pilot asked air traffic control about an unexplained traffic advisory near Baltimore and received an answer that probably was not what he was expecting: there had been “alien sightings” in the area. The exchange makes for entertaining listening, though the actual report is considerably less dramatic.

A recording circulating online captures an unusual conversation reportedly involving American Eagle flight 5432 from Washington National (DCA) to Philadelphia (PHL) on November 21, 2026.

According to International Business Times, PSA Airlines operated the flight with a Bombardier CRJ-900, using the callsign Blue Streak 5432. Near Baltimore, the pilot asked about a traffic advisory without an identification tag. The controller explained that the flight had already passed the only other known traffic nearby.

“I mean, we have had alien sightings out there, so…”

The controller went on to describe an earlier report from another pilot about something zigzagging ahead of an aircraft near Martin State Airport, without a corresponding radar target.

The American Eagle pilot took the comment in good humor, suggesting it would make an interesting story to tell his family.

A pilot reporting strange lights near Baltimore got an unexpected response from ATC, who casually mentioned there had been alien sightings in the area. The pilot joked that he’d have quite the story to tell his family. 👽✈️#ATC #Aviation #Aliens pic.twitter.com/rtalRieUwH

— Flightdrama (@flightdrama) November 21, 2026

Before you start booking a window seat from BWI specifically to look for visitors from another planet, the American Eagle crew was asking about a traffic advisory… these pilots did not actually see an unidentified object outside their aircraft.

The zigzagging object was part of the controller’s recollection of a different pilot’s report: there’s quite a leap from an unexplained alert and a controller’s remark to an extraterrestrial encounter.

Yet after so much grim aviation news lately, I enjoyed this one.

Pilots and controllers have serious responsibilities, but there is room for a little personality on the frequency when circumstances permit. It is often the testy verbal exchanges between pilots and air traffic controllers that make headlines, but a passing remark like this also gives us a glimpse of the human beings doing the work.

An American Eagle pilot’s question about a traffic advisory prompted an unexpected reference to earlier alien sightings near Baltimore. While there was no alien spacecraft sighting, it is an entertaining radio exchange and a rather good story.

#6147. Craving an Island Escape? These Bahamas Airbnbs Are Just What the Doctor Ordered

Growing up in Fort Lauderdale, the Bahamas always felt like an extension of South Florida to me. Just a short flight or boat ride away, the archipelago was somewhere I returned to often, and still do. Yet what continues to surprise me is how different one island can feel from the next. I've always thought it was a shame that so many visitors to the Bahamas never make it beyond Nassau or Freeport. Eleuthera has some of the prettiest beaches I've seen, the water around the Exumas is almost unbelievably clear, and the Abacos have small waterfront towns that are worth exploring. Each island has its own personality, and even after years of visiting, there are so many I still want to discover.

Renting a home is one of my favorite ways to experience it all. Beautiful beachfront villas, colorful cottages, and contemporary homes with pools overlooking the sea are everywhere in the Bahamas. Having your own place makes it easy to settle in, explore a little, and enjoy the particular rhythm of whichever island you've chosen. After so many visits, I’m eager to step slightly off the typical tourist path (although the resorts and hotels here are also beautiful), and these Bahamas Airbnbs are a great way to do so. Read on for my most-recommended rentals in the Bahamas, from beachfront stays to island cottages.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 12 (up to 8 adults and 4 children)Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Heated pool, direct beach access, bohemian interiors

With its natural textures, airy interiors, and covered outdoor lounge, Corsair Key feels specially designed for long, unhurried days by the water. Four king bedrooms offer plenty of room for families or friends, while a heated swimming pool and direct beach access make it tempting to stay put. The well-equipped kitchen and generous dining spaces are especially appealing for groups who enjoy cooking together. And with a location in Bimini (the westernmost district of The Bahamas) being so close to South Florida, getting here is surprisingly easy.

Location: Rockwell Island, BiminiThings to do nearby: Radio Beach, Bimini snorkeling, fishing excursions

Check Availability at Homes and Villas by Marriott

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 5.5 bathsWhy we love it: Retro design, heated pool, outdoor grill that looks like a vintage VW bus

A vintage Volkswagen bus turned barbecue station isn't something you expect to find at a luxury vacation rental, but that's part of the fun at this quirky, vibrant spot. This five-bedroom bungalow embraces its retro personality with bold artwork, wicker lighting, and colorful bedrooms. Outside, a heated pool is surrounded by tropical landscaping, while Harbour Island's famous pink sands are just a short walk away. It's a playful alternative to more traditional island cottages, with enough room for the whole family; kids will particularly love the bunk beds.

Location: Dunmore Town, Harbour IslandThings to do nearby: Pink Sand Beach, Dunmore Town, Briland's Blue Hole

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Direct beachfront access, waterfront deck, panoramic views

The best feature of this three-bedroom cottage? The uninterrupted sea views, visible through expansive windows and from the waterfront deck. The interiors are simple and contemporary, with an open living space that keeps the focus firmly on the scenery. Spend the morning swimming, take a drive to Tropic of Cancer Beach, or settle in with a book and watch the water change color throughout the afternoon. With three bedrooms—a king, a queen, and a room with a queen and a lofted twin—the property sleeps up to seven.

Location: Moore Hill, Little ExumaThings to do nearby: Tropic of Cancer Beach, Santana's Grill Pit, Little Exuma beaches

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Infinity pool, private cinema, ocean views

Location: Aqualina, NassauThings to do nearby: Cable Beach, Baha Mar, Nassau boat excursions

Check Availability at Marriott Home and Villas

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private pool, beachfront setting, covered oceanfront terrace

Vaulted wood ceilings and enormous windows bring warmth and light to this four-bedroom home on Tar Bay, but the outdoor spaces are what make Aquamarine Villa particularly appealing. A private swimming pool overlooks the beach, while a shaded terrace offers a welcome escape from the afternoon sun. The open-plan living area makes gathering easy, and the bedroom configuration—two kings with oceanfront views, a queen, and a room with a queen and a bunk bed—works well for families traveling together. With the sand just steps past the pool, shoes are likely to remain optional for most of the stay.

Location: Tar Bay, Great ExumaThings to do nearby: Hoopers Bay, George Town, Exuma boat excursions

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pink-sand beach, heated pool, covered veranda

Neighborhood: Governor's Harbour area, EleutheraThings to do nearby: Pink-sand beaches, Governor's Harbour, local snorkeling

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Private waterfront deck, bedroom ocean views, optional private chef

Some of the best places to stay in the Bahamas are the ones that make you feel completely surrounded by water. At this intimate one-bedroom retreat on Exuma, enormous bedroom windows look directly toward the sea, and a private deck provides access to the water below. The interiors are understated, with a kitchenette designed for light meals rather than elaborate cooking. A private chef can be arranged for dinner for an added fee, or guests can venture into nearby George Town for a delicious meal at one of the waterfront restaurants.

Location: Near George Town, ExumaThings to do nearby: George Town waterfront, snorkeling, Exuma boat excursions

Number of guests: 14Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Private pool, beachfront location, kayaks and paddleboards

Sea turtles frequently visit the shallow waters of Hoopers Bay, and guests at Blu Wakes have an excellent vantage point for spotting them. The five-bedroom villa—four kings and a room for kids with two queens and a bunk bed—opens onto a beautiful stretch of beach, with a private pool overlooking the water. Kayaks and paddleboards make it easy to explore the bay, while concierge services can arrange everything from a private chef to a day trip exploring the Exuma cays. With room for 14, it's particularly well suited to extended families or big groups.

Location: Hoopers Bay, Great ExumaThings to do nearby: Hoopers Bay sea turtles, George Town, Exuma cays excursions

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beachfront location, porch, on-site beach bar

There's a clear appeal to a place like this where the biggest morning decision is whether to take your coffee on the porch or at the beach. This cheerful little cottage, called Tiny's Toes in the Sand, has rocking chairs overlooking Salt Pond Harbour, a kitchenette for simple meals, and a beach bar just steps away. At only 400 square feet, it's not a place for spreading out, but for two people looking to spend most of their time steps from the water, that's rather the point.

Location: Salt Pond, Long IslandThings to do nearby: Salt Pond Harbour, Dean's Blue Hole, Cape Santa Maria Beach

Number of guests: 16Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 9 bathsWhy we love it: Infinity pool, outdoor kitchen, concierge services

With seven bedrooms and more than 5,000 square feet of living space, Sea Salt Villa is designed for a crowd. The contemporary home sits within a gated community overlooking Emerald Bay, with expansive windows, an infinity pool, and a covered outdoor entertaining area. An outdoor kitchen makes casual dinners easy, while concierge services can help arrange private chefs and excursions. It's a particularly good option for extended families or groups of friends who want the space of a private home but still enjoy resort-style comforts. Plus, it’s located on a PGA golf course if you’re looking to get in a round or two, and guests can rent golf carts to drive around the community.

Location: Emerald Bay, Great ExumaThings to do nearby: Emerald Bay Beach, golf, Exuma boat excursions

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Bayfront balcony, rooftop sunset views, walkable location

There's a lovely sense of everyday island life at this two-bedroom apartment overlooking Anchor Bay. From the balcony, guests can watch boats coming and going, while the shared rooftop gallery is a particularly nice place to catch the sunset. The apartment has a well-equipped kitchen and two en suite bedrooms, and restaurants and shops are within walking distance. Beach chairs, towels, and a cooler are provided for exploring Eleuthera's coastline, making it easy to head out for the day.

Location: Governor's Harbour, EleutheraThings to do nearby: French Leave Beach, Haynes Library, Governor's Harbour restaurants

#6145. Review: Air France A350-900 Business Class Paris To New York

Air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to New York. The new A350-900 cabin is excellent, but what impressed me most was how well everything came together, from the comfortable seat to the delicious dinner, gracious service, and fast Starlink Wi-Fi.

I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe. Having had more time to reflect on it, I stand by that assessment…this flight left very little room for improvement.

I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer. Flying Blue came through with a last-minute business class award from Basel to Paris to New York for 60,000 miles plus €453 in taxes and fees. The timing worked perfectly and I booked this about 36-hour before departure, so saver space can certainly open up via FlyingBlue.

This was a so-called “reverse redeye,” leaving Europe late in the evening and arriving in the United States even later that same evening. That suited my plans very well, particularly because I had an overnight drive to Pittsburgh ahead of me after landing.

My journey began in Basel with an Air France Hop! flight to Paris. I had time to visit the lounge before my connection and enjoyed a meal there, though I deliberately left room for dinner onboard.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in 6L. Though approaching 8:00 pm, it was still very light outside.

I first reviewed Air France A350 business class in 2020, flying from Paris to Toronto. I enjoyed that flight very much, but the newer business class cabin represents a substantial improvement.

Far more important the gimmicky door was the room for your feet, which I found plentiful. Legroom is 43 inches when the seat is the upright position and it transforms into a bed that is 79 inches long. Seats are 21 inches wide.

There are no personal art vents, but thankfully the cabin was kept very chilly. I also loved the window darkening feature, where the window tinting could be adjusted simply by sliding your finger left or right.

I found this suite spacious and comfortable whether sitting upright, reclining, or lying down. The cabin looks so sharp. I particularly love the illuminated winged seahorse at each seat…a small detail, but one that gives the cabin an unmistakable Air France identity.

There was plenty of personal storage, and the wireless charging worked well, though there was also USB-C and universal A/C power.

After dinner, I converted my seat into a bed and slept for about four hours.

The Sofitel-branded bedding (duvet, mattress pad, pillow) was excellent, and I found the seat very comfortable for sleeping.

This is one of my favorite business class seats.

Air France provided a very attractive amenity kit with an embossed seahorse on the bag. It was lined with red and the contents included:

The catering was a highlight of this flight. I had eaten in the lounge, but was very glad I saved room for dinner.

Before takeoff, flight attendants offered Champagne and a warm towel, along with the familiar Gavottes savory biscuits.

The full menu (every menu item and ingredient is French except for Coca-Cola):

Dinner began with an appetizer of pea, lemon, and basil cream accompanied by smoked salmon fillet and raspberry and grapefruit jelly.

A side salad accompanied the starter, though I saved mine until after the main course, as the French do. The bread was delicious.

I also tried the Quintessence cocktail, an Air France variation on a Negroni. It combined La Quintinye royal red vermouth, bitter Chambéry liqueur, a hint of fig, and ABK6 VSOP Cognac. I enjoyed it very much. It was not nearly as strong as a traditional Negroni, which suited me just fine on this flight.

For my main course, I chose veal with a creamy morel mushroom sauce, spelt risotto, and peas.

Admittedly, the presentation was not going to win any awards…yes, it looked like vomit. But it tasted delicious and I would happily order it again. I enjoyed a delicious glass of Chateau D’Arsac wine, which was so good.

A cheese course followed, then dessert. I enjoyed both ice cream and a crispy hazelnut tart, accompanied by hot chocolate.

This was a substantial supper and a very satisfying one.

About an hour before landing, flight attendants served a light meal of shrimp with a pickled cucumber salad.

It was excellent and just the right amount of food after the large dinner. I had two espressos with it, which helped prepare me for the late night ahead.

The entertainment system included a tail camera, which I particularly enjoyed during our departure from Paris (though not the fire that seemed to be burning near CDG). It was a gorgeous evening, and watching the aircraft leave Charles de Gaulle was a lovely way to begin the flight.

I did not watch any movies or TV on this flight, but there was large selection of movies, TV shows, games, and music.

Noise-cancelling headphones were provided, though you can also connect your own Bluetooth device.

Fast, free Starlink internet was available onboard. The connection worked from gate to gate and felt much like using the internet on the ground. I did not have any essential work to complete on this flight, but I appreciated being able to connect onboard. Starlink increasingly influences which flights I book. Air France already gives me plenty of reasons to choose it, but reliable internet makes the proposition even more attractive, especially for a daytime westbound journey when I might otherwise spend several hours working.

The Air France A350 has three lavatories in business class: one I the front (though typically reserved for crew use) and two in between the front and rear cabin.

Service was warm and attentive throughout the flight. I was even addressed by surname.

I have heard plenty of complaints over the years about service on Air France, but my own experiences have been very positive. This crew continued that pattern and the great service complemented the rest of the experience. I enjoyed a delicious meal, slept comfortably, and felt well cared for throughout the journey.

The new seat deserves attention, but a cabin can only do so much without a good crew in terms of leaving a lasting positive impression. On this flight, Air France delivered both.

We landed on time at JFK, and I quickly cleared immigration using Global Entry. The late arrival had been part of the appeal when booking, and the flight delivered exactly what I had hoped for: an enjoyable evening onboard, a few hours of rest, and an on-time arrival in New York.

Then it was time to collect a rental car and begin my overnight drive to Pittsburgh…

This was a tremendous flight on Air France…I have no complaints at all about anything.

I liked the older A350 business class product when I flew it in 2020, but the newer seat is a considerable improvement. Pair that with excellent bedding, delicious food, and a gracious crew, then add Starlink, and I struggle to identify much that I would change. Cappuccinos maybe that are not powdered?

The lack of individual air vents remains a drawback, though the comfortable cabin temperature thankfully meant it did not interfere with my sleep on this flight.

Air France reminded me how enjoyable a transatlantic business class flight can be when the airline gets the details right. I would happily book this product again and would go out of my way to find it.

#6144. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

New customers, listen up: Away often offers a 10% off coupon on first orders when you sign up for emails and texts. This coupon code is not currently being offered, but keep your eyes peeled for its return. Once signed up, you'll stay in the loop on the latest launches and collabs, special events, and more. To snag the deal, head to Away's homepage and keep an out for a pop-up, then enter your information to sign up.

Away is making travel more accessible for those who give back to their communities with a 10% discount for veterans, active military members, medical personnel, teachers, and students. Whether you're a student preparing for a semester abroad or a teacher gearing up for a well-deserved getaway, this offer makes premium luggage more affordable. Simply verify your status through ID.me, and you’re all set to enjoy stylish, durable travel essentials at a discounted price. For more details, visit Away’s Hero Discounts.

Sharing your love of travel has its perks with Away’s $40 off referral offer. When you introduce a friend to the brand, they’ll receive $40 off their first purchase of $125 or more—and once their order is complete, you’ll get $40 off your next one, too. The best part?
