#6141. FAA Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Week in 16 Years

More than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

Air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA said, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials said they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

“Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”

The FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

#6139. The 40 Best Resorts in the Caribbean: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year, our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best resorts in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View this gallery as a list of the top resorts in the Caribbean with scores here.

The namesake hillside resort set above Toiny Bay gives “wild” an unexpected new meaning when it comes to sceney St. Barts. On the shrubby southeastern point of the island, this unfussy haven is where an in-the-know social set head to find serenity. The star amenity here is the private beach, accessible via a three-minute Defender ride down switchbacking roads. Le Toiny’s stretch of soft sand is considered the sole private hotel beach on all of St. Barts. Plus, some of the oldest traditional English-style cottages on the island, dating back to the 1700s, can be found beside the beach club (one is currently used as treatment areas for the spa). The suites and villas were redesigned in 2024 to create airy living spaces that draw your eye outward to the leafy open-air surroundings and azure water views just beyond your private pool deck.

Grand Cayman may be famous for its SCUBA diving and offshore banking, but with several daily non-stops from New York and Boston, it’s increasingly drawing families to its powdery, placid western Caribbean beaches. On the island’s Seven Mile Beach—one of the loveliest stretches of sand in the world—you'll find the 266-room Kimpton Seafire Resort & Spa, with a boutique atmosphere that manages to be both child-friendly (two pools, a kids club) and hip (colorful, contemporary design, and a lobby scene replete with pool table, library, and daily happy hour). The food is also strong: Hit beachside Coccoloba for fish tacos and ceviches; Ave, the resort's primary restaurant, for epic breakfast buffets (including house-made cronuts); and the sceney Avecita for progressive Spanish fare like white anchovy toast and prawn tartare, served up alongside craft cocktails at the chef’s counter. You can always snorkel and parasail right off the hotel’s beach, but you’re also just a short ride from Stingray City (where you can stand on a sandbar and touch giant rays as they swim by), world-class gardens (look for the endangered blue iguana), golf, and roadside jerk chicken. Hit Rum Point to toast the sunset—or maybe you'll prefer doing that from your own private balcony.

This romantic all-suite beachfront retreat north of the sprawling all-inclusives of Punta Cana is a diamond literally in the rough—the last two miles of the approach road are so bone rattling that it may be worth ponying up more than $250 for the ten-minute helicopter transfer from the airport in Punta Cana. But behind the resort’s unmarked security gate, Zoëtry is breathtaking. The open-air lobby has a soaring peaked thatch roof, and the 51rooms, divided between two-story thatched buildings and freestanding villas, are arranged around two snaking pools and are no more than a one-minute walk from the beach. With classic clean lines, they are dramatic by virtue of their size (the smallest is 775 square feet) and simple comforts—wicker ceilings, dark hardwood floors and furniture, white-on-white beds, immense bathrooms with black slate showers and deep soaking tubs. The resort’s restaurants draw culinary inspiration from traditional Dominican fare and international flavors, with an emphasis on using locally grown and organic ingredients.

For toes-in-the-sand luxury with impeccable service, foodie-approved eateries, Caribbean-cool rooms, and views that will have all your friends and family seeing green, La Samanna can’t be beat. Set along the white sands of Baie Longue, known for being one of the most beautiful beaches in all of St. Martin, guests are never far from the startlingly turquoise waters, and La Samanna offers plenty of ways to get out on the water, including complimentary kayaks, paddleboards, snorkeling gear, and more. With three main restaurants—one of which changes in concept between lunch and dinner—plus a fabulous daily breakfast and top-notch room service, there’s really no reason to leave for meals. The star of the show is L’Oursin, the upscale French restaurant just off the lobby, where each table comes with a view of the sailboat-spotted sea. If you can, splurge on one of the property's eight independent villas—the double-level mansions have everything a group could need to vacation more than comfortably.

The "secret" part of Secret Bay's name is no accident—the resort's 10 gorgeous villas give new meaning to the word hideaway. Touches vary from villa to villa, but all have interiors and floors made of Guyanese Greenheart, bedroom furniture made of Dominican red cedar, open decks, private pools, and 180-degree views over the mountain peaks of Dominica and the Caribbean Sea. Though we doubt you'll get tired of living your own castaway fantasies (albeit with much nicer accommodations), Secret Bay's concierge is available to help craft personalized itineraries: think rainforest hikes with a famed naturalist, or a sunset sail along the island's western coast.

Anguilla is a small-but-mighty island packed with a handful of luxury properties, dining options, and a whole bunch of outstanding beaches. Barnes Bay and Meads Bay surround the property on both sides, with waters that are occasionally rough but known to be swimmable at other times of the year. Regardless of the conditions, white beach chairs line the sand in pristine formation each morning, and three large pool areas—two kid-friendly, and one adults-only—provide plenty of swimming options when the ocean is unavailable. The property stretches across the shore, which means each room provides a unique view of some combination of the wide property’s beachfront, ocean, palm trees, or garden areas. In the ocean-view one-bedroom suite, we overlooked the modernist pool deck as well as the distant ocean, with a plunge pool on the balcony and ample outdoor space for afternoon lounging. The bathroom was equipped with two sinks, a large tub, and a marble walk-in shower.

All rooms at this Sandals Resort are in stone buildings on a two-mile-long beach in a 500-acre wilderness preserve on the island's south coast. The resort is arranged as three European villages—Dutch, French, and Italian (including a Venetian piazza)—and the architecture includes lots of marble columns and vaulted ceilings. "Buildings are spread out, but it still feels like an intimate retreat." Rooms differ according to village: French rooms have mahogany four-poster beds and Caribbean decor, while Italian rooms are heavy on marble. The plantation-style Eleanor's, complete with a waterwheel and a stone fireplace, serves contemporary Caribbean cuisine.

Though the Buccaneer, on the U.S. Virgin Island of St. Croix, has been proudly run by the Armstrong family for over 70 years—it's the longest-running resort in the Caribbean—its history dates even further back to the property's earliest construction by a Knight of Malta in 1653. Since then, it's been a private home; a sugar mill; a cotton estate, then a cattle estate; and now, an incredibly warm, family-friendly resort that's more like a country club. You have access to an 18-hole golf course, eight tennis courts, three beaches (whether you prefer kayaking and snorkeling or lounging in peace and quiet), a full water sports center, and none of the pretense. Arrive for lunch at the Grotto in your bathing suit, and please don't sleep through the terrific breakfast buffet. The Buccanneer knows how to put out a spread. Once you're done moving about for the day, settle into the deluxe oceanfront room—the resort's most popular—and lie on your bed beneath the 16-foot-high wood ceilings, watching the waves lap the beach out your picture window.

The tiny volcanic island of Grenada is both an unexpected and obvious choice for Six Senses’ foray into the Caribbean. Compared to big-hitting neighbors like St. Lucia and Antigua, it has been overlooked by travelers to the region. But this means that it remains largely uncrowded and retains a more rustic version of tourism. Six Senses has done well to anchor itself to that. Here, your welcome ritual begins with a sensory spice “tour;” its 56 suites and 15 villas are stylish but designed to sit unobtrusively on the landscape; and its curated excursions—from rainforest hikes to Rastafarian farm visits—spotlight the best of Grenada’s natural bounty. In classic Six Senses style, wellness is a key protagonist, and you can seek out everything from aerial yoga to sleep therapy, as well as treatments like the Caribbean Cleansing Ritual that nod to the surroundings. It’s very tempting to stay put, heading to the spa or sipping rum cocktails poolside, but you’d do well to pair off with one of the property’s community hosts and head out: to spice-laden markets in its photogenic capital or for a bit of beachside limin’ (defined locally as “kicking with friends”), a beloved national pastime.

The old adage of getting what you pay for rings true here, and while it may be a splurge, it will be an unforgettable stay. The rooms are quiet, the beds are comfortable, and in my opinion, this is the best stretch of beach on the island. If you’re looking for luxury—and budget isn’t an issue—the Ritz is the top of the line. Guests who stay in the 320 spacious and chic rooms can expect to be spoiled. Servers cruise around the shore on Segway scooters, effortlessly balancing trays of tropical cocktails. The concierge can secure reservations for you at sold-out restaurants, set up offsite tours, and suggest itineraries for any kind of traveler. The 15,000-square-foot spa at the Ritz is one of the largest and best on the island, and the property's on-site restaurants are simply divine. The vibe is upscale without being stuffy, with guests in the elevators side by side wearing pool towels and Prada.

A relatively new addition to St. Barts' luxury hotel scene, Le Barthélemy is a sophisticated winner that keeps with the island's low-rise sensibility. Set between a lagoon and Grand Cul-de-Sac beach along the island's northeastern shore, the hotel is an education in understated elegance. Rooms are spare and enormous, with lots of wood and one or two pops of bright color—some even have small, rectangular plunge pools for mini-laps. The food at  Amis St. Barth is unabashedly modern French, with attention paid to proper portions in the tropics: in other words, not too much. Water sports enthusiasts have an expanse of calm shallow waters for kayaking, kite-surfing, and snorkeling—a flotilla of a dozen sea turtles that survived the storms of 2017 remain in residence and are easily visible.

Those who knew and loved Le Carl Gustaf the first time around will have even more reason to fall for it now that the Barriere group has taken over. The hotelier company—known for reviving particularly beloved but withering properties—has made sure to keep the spirit of Le Carl chic and easy. The raw wood and petite terraces still make it feel like the beach house of a fabulous French friend, yet the hotel’s reimagined approach to the environment gives it a 21st-century edge. Paris design firm Gilles and Boissier gussied up the 21 rooms with creams, stone, and linen, as well as a profusion of palms separating various spaces with a curtain of greenery. Suites have been reconfigured to catch sea breezes, providing natural air conditioning. And a fleet of electric bikes brings guests down the hill upon which the hotel stands like a lookout, over the town and coastline, to nearby Shell Beach, the perfect place for a picnic prepared by the hotel’s staff that feels, appropriately simple and chic—much like Le Carl itself.

Romance is taken to a whole other level at this adults-only St. Lucia resort. With 36 plunge pool suites, butler service, and a personalized bar with only the top-shelf, this enclave was made for couples to relax and reconnect. While there's no shortage of places to lounge or splash around in on property, the resort also offers an array of excursions to explore the gorgeous corner of the Caribbean St. Lucia lays claim to. From rainforest nature walks with a fully packed picnic basket to adrenaline-pumping ATV tours, Serenity at Coconut Bay knows there's many ways to take in all the gorgeous scenery.

#6138. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#6137. My Favorite Villa: A Storybook Trullo in Puglia With Six Bedrooms, a Private Chef, and Olive Grove Views

My best friend and I had an entire six-bedroom estate in Puglia, Italy, to ourselves for three nights in early November. We could have invited another 10 people, but there was something rather wonderful about having all that space for just the two of us. The region's whitewashed streets had emptied of their summer crowds, and the countryside around our home away from home was quiet enough that we felt no particular urgency to go anywhere.

I'd been looking forward to sleeping in a trullo, one of the traditional dry-stone houses with conical roofs that dot this part of southern Italy. At Trullo delle Dame, my bedroom sat directly beneath one of those cones, and every night, I fell asleep looking up at the curved stone ceiling. It felt like a storybook hideaway reimagined by someone with a very good eye for design. The soaking tub in my room didn't hurt either.

The original stone walls and domed ceilings have been preserved throughout the restored trulli, with sleek off-white furniture, stone walls, and traditional glazed ceramic or terra-cotta ornaments called pumi strewn about. The six bedrooms, including five en suite bedrooms and a primary suite, are spread out across the property. While I was there with my friend, I kept thinking about how well the house would work for a multigenerational family trip. There's enough space for everyone to retreat to their own rooms, and plenty of reasons to come back together over a chef-prepared meal, a card game in the seating area overlooking the countryside, or a dip in the saltwater infinity pool.

My favorite spot in the estate was the outdoor kitchen—specifically at the enormous round dining table, complete with a giant lazy Susan. One afternoon, we made orecchiette there, shaping the little ears of pasta by hand, flour up to our wrists, before sitting down to eat what we'd made. I could picture a dozen people around that table on a summer evening, passing plates of pasta and pouring each other another glass of wine (which the Mandarin Oriental team will stock the fridge with upon request).

Throughout the stay, our days fell into an easy routine. We'd walk through the olive groves in the mornings, read on the couch in the afternoons, and spend a few hours on the loungers by the pool. The water was unheated, so we were content to stay poolside in November. But I imagine it's where everyone ends up in July.

As tempting as it was to stay put, there was too much good food and wine in the surrounding countryside to spend all three days at the house. We drove the three miles into Cisternino for a meal at Taverna della Torre, and I'm still thinking about the gnocchi with white truffles. Another afternoon took us to Giovanni Aiello, an independent winery near Putignano, where we got to help make some of the bottle labels. The cellar is beautiful, and you can even have your tasting inside an old wine barrel. With the towns of Martina Franca and Ostuni also within easy driving distance, we could have happily spent a few more days eating our way around Puglia.

Some little bites, courtesy of the private chef

Of course, we hardly needed to leave the house to eat well. Each morning, our private chef laid out a breakfast spread of fresh yogurt, meats and cheeses, pies, pancakes, juices, and fruit, along with freshly brewed cappuccinos. There was enough food to feed considerably more than two people, though we did our best. In the evenings, he prepared multicourse dinners using local, seasonal produce. Of everything he made, my favorite was a fava bean purée with roasted peppers.

As two busy working moms, we quickly got used to the luxury of not having to think about what anyone would eat. Waking up to a breakfast feast and a creamy coffee, knowing someone else would deal with the dishes, was perhaps the hardest thing to give up at the end of the trip. (My family may need to lower their breakfast expectations for the foreseeable future.) And while we thoroughly enjoyed our few days off from mom duties, I could see how having a chef would make a family vacation feel much more like a vacation for the parents too. No grocery runs, no figuring out what to cook for 12 people, and no kitchen to clean up afterward.

The writer participating in a pasta-making class in the outdoor kitchen

The fruits of their labor: lots of orecchiette!

If we came back with our kids, I'd happily sign them up for a pizza-making session while we snuck off for a massage in the olive groves, all activities the brand offers to guests. The trees, which produce the estate's own olive oil, also make a rather lovely setting for a yoga class, which can also be arranged during the warmer months.

A few things worth knowing before booking: The private chef, food, and drinks are charged separately from the villa rental. You'll also want a car to explore the neighboring towns, although the concierge can arrange transfers. And if you're coming in November, as we did, check restaurant opening hours before heading out, since some places shorten their hours after the summer season. The unheated pool is also worth keeping in mind if you're traveling with children outside the warmer months.

On the morning we left, our chef packed us meat-and-cheese sandwiches for the road. After three days of elaborate breakfasts and multicourse dinners, those sandwiches somehow ranked among my favorite things he'd made. As we drove away, I thought about how I'd happily come back with a houseful of friends and family in summer—but I'd want the same bedroom under the cone.

#6136. A Real-Life Santa’s Workshop: How Macy’s Parade Studio Works All Year to Prep for Thanksgiving Day Magic

Santa’s workshop just might be inside a rather plain red-and-black brick building in northern New Jersey. Sitting about 10 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan in Moonachie’s industrial park district, the 72,000-square-foot warehouse is home to Macy’s Parade Studio, where 60 designers, carpenters, welders, seamstresses, and other artisans chip away year-round to prepare for one morning a year: the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

This year, the festivities are grander than ever, as the team has toiled for two years in preparation for a major milestone: the parade’s 100th edition. Instead of the normal 50 to 60 inflatables, there will be nearly 100. The usual 500 new costumes will be upped to 1,000, while more than 11,000 volunteers will be a part of the milestone event.

A snapshot of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from 1940

It’s a massive endeavor for a tradition that started as a two-block-long procession of Central Park Zoo animals, a handful of bands, and Santa, all traveling six miles from Harlem to the department store’s flagship in Herald Square at 34th and Broadway in 1924 (it was suspended for three years during World War II from 1942 to 1944). The parade led to the unveiling of Macy’s window displays with puppets by marionette artist Tony Sarg to kick off the holiday—and retail—season.

“It started as a bunch of Macy's immigrant coworkers coming together to create a party like they had in their home countries,” Brendan Kennedy, director of creative production, tells me during a visit in late September. But soon, the animals were deemed to be “too scary” for children. Three years later, the balloons debuted, the work of Sarg, who he calls “one of the godfathers of puppetry” and “our Walt Disney.” His genius idea: flip marionettes upside down to become high-flying balloons on strings, creating the iconic tradition we know today.

Taking a peek at the concept art hanging inside the Macy's workshop

Wandering through the facility is like making your way through a pop culture fun house. A pair of Minions hang from the rafters, mingling with Pokémon’s Pikachu and Goofy, who is stuck in a wreath. A Planter’s Peanut Ferris wheel spins in the center, while models of the parade’s own famous characters, Tom Turkey, Blue Hippopotamus, and the fishy pair Rainbow and Greybow Trout, sit out to dry in front of shelves lined with paint buckets of every hue.

“This is like our own Hollywood lot,” Kennedy says. Indeed, there’s the distinct feel of a soundstage paired with the wildest arts and crafts studio you've ever seen, all together feeling like something out of Willy Wonka’s dreams. Before making its home here in 2011, the Parade Studio was located inside the old Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, New Jersey, for decades.

Despite the holiday joy bursting from every seam, parade preparation is serious business. Every single element is handcrafted and hand-painted. "Generally it all starts with a napkin sketch,” Kennedy explains of the initial rough drawing. “It goes into full modeling in 3-D, and then engineering, where we have to figure out how to get this thing into the real world.”

But year after year, like the true elves of the holiday season they are, they pull it off—testing every float and balloon for any and every possible weather condition—so that on Thanksgiving morning, the 3.5 million lining the Manhattan route as well as the nearly 35 million watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade at home (airing on NBC and Peacock from 8:30 a.m. to noon) can just sit back and revel in the delights of the season.

“What makes the parade so special is that it is an event that has been produced by colleagues since it began in 1924, and it continues to be Macy Studios colleagues' gift to New York City and gift to people who are tuning in around the country to watch on television,” Macy’s director of production operations Kathleen Wright tells Traveler.

Below, we peek behind the scenes of the Macy’s Parade Studio as the team prepares for the 100th parade, and how they plan to honor the traditions of the last century.

Some of the 3-D printed models that serve as the blueprints for the parade's iconic floats

The larger-than-life magic of the parade starts on the smallest scale. In the Studio’s 3-D print room, nearly a dozen machines hum away, creating miniature models—the first step in conceiving how to build each float. But that’s not the only tool used. Recently, engineers and sculptors have turned to augmented reality goggles, not just to picture the elements, but even wearing them while sculpting to make sure they get details right in a 3-D space.

The day I visit, the team is problem-solving on the new Purina Dog Chow Salute to Service Dogs float, which features three oversized dog puppets.

An array of the painted models inside the studio

“When floats come to life through some sort of animation is when it’s at its peak,” Kennedy says. While animatronics could provide the movements, they would lack the human touch. “With a puppet, I can look directly at you, give you a little show, and then pan to the next person. You get a lot more energy and excitement. There’s a long history of puppetry in the parade, so we made a concerted effort to include it.”

The team works through solutions for the best way to have a puppeteer lie below the float bed, controlling the motions from below while positioned with body pillows that still allow them to see the parade-goers through a scrim. They consider using delivery truck slats to increase the height of the float so the puppeteer can remain comfortable and still operate the puppet.

Mr. Peanut is the historic parade's oldest character.

In another section, another new float is going for a test spin. Planters’ Mr. Peanut Power Plant will celebrate the parade’s oldest character, with peanut-shaped confetti erupting through his top hat, as well as a rotating Ferris wheel showcasing his evolution from 1916, starting with the napkin sketch created by a 13-year-old boy from Virginia.

Also on the floor is a puppet of the original character Mr. Inspector, a stern-looking comic book character with a top hat and magnifying glass, who first appeared as a balloon in the 1929 parade. This version of the character was taken out of the archives and freshened up in order to be part of Macy’s own Tony Sarg’s Amazing Marionettes float.

“Everything has to be refurbished,” Kennedy says. “These are New York City streets—it’s not like a perfect Narnia land. So they hit a bump, we have to work through it, or if it rains, we have to check for water damage.”

While the methods are precise, the methodology is all about creativity and resourcefulness. Case in point: While working on the Wednesday Addams float in 2024, Tim Burton himself asked for more decay and rot. So a sculptor modified his glue gun to spray spider webs around the entire float. “It’s a good example of how anything can become a tool,” he says of making fiction come to life.

But there are some strict restrictions. Floats have to fold up to the size of a standard city bus in order to fit through the Lincoln Tunnel into Manhattan. The massive convoy travels in two nights before Thanksgiving. Once settled, the team reassembles every piece, some using cranes, as every float gets its final touches before the big day.

Peeking inside the planning of the parade's Mickey Mouse float

Next, we step into the Balloon Studio, where again, everything starts with a 3-D model. After it’s approved, a larger form “white model,” roughly a few feet long, is generated (clay models were used in the past) and used to hand-draw lines that determine the shapes and sizes of each piece of balloon fabric that needs to be cut and how they’ll be melded together, much like sewing with a dress pattern.

Dangling from beams above is a display of white models of the past, with the monotone versions of Super Mario, Buzz Lightyear, Snoopy, and the Pillsbury Doughboy, among others. But today the focus is on the freshly-completed Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey Mouse, hanging from a little stand to mimic levitation. I count no less than nine pieces of fabric sketched out in pencil just for the nose—and about 18 for the front side of each ear.

Artisans stitch together all the massive textiles that go onto the floats.

At the next station, we see a pair of artisans doing seemingly mundane work stitching large swaths of fabric together with sewing machines. To a trained eye, though, the scene is actually chock full of proprietary Macy’s secrets. While rubber was used in the past, today the balloons are made of off-white secret material the makeup of which is closely guarded. The material is heat-sealed together using these Macy’s-designed machines with wheels that heat up to 410 degrees Fahrenheit. Then the material is painted using a formula that’s also—you guessed it—proprietary.

The secrets all come together as the completed balloons are first inflated indoors to make sure that the paint looks good and to check how it behaves with air. Some are inspected in the Studio while others that require more space are pumped up from the floor since it would float at the nearby Prudential Center. The balloons are inflated at various stages to ensure the air is filling up as intended.

The big test came on November 7, when they hosted the annual Balloonfest at MetLife Stadium to see how the balloons behave in outdoor conditions, as well as give city agencies the chance to approve everything.

Once that’s checked off, the night before the parade is the Balloon Inflation (which is open to the public; stay tuned for details here), when each character is blown up on the streets of the Upper West Side and prepped for its own turkey trot through Midtown. “They really are flying pieces of art,” Kennedy says.

A dress from the costume operations studio

While the floats and balloons may get the headlines, there would be no parade without the nearly 11,000 volunteers who help make the day happen, which is now 2.5-miles from the Upper West Side to Herald Square—and they all have to be dressed for the occasion. This year at least 1,500 more costumes are needed, but that doesn't intimidate costume director and associate producer Kimberly Montgomery, who’s been doing this for 27 years. “It’s gone so fast because it’s just been so darn fun,” she says of her tenure.

Costumes follow after the design of the float, with the larger backdrop serving as the source of wardrobe inspiration.

Every costume always begins in the same place. “We start with the design of the float and then riff off of that to tell a story with live people,” she explains. Just then, she catches a glimpse of a new design of a float with street signs and immediately starts brainstorming: “Maybe people on bikes will give it some texture and energy.” After all, she sees the floats as roving stages. "They're like mini Broadway shows.”

When the very first 1924 parade arrived at Macy’s, it was met by employees dressed as clowns—and this year there will be 1,000 clowns throughout the parade, just a portion of the costume packets that she’s been working all year to assemble. And it's not just with what they'll wear. The late November weather is a major consideration as well. Costume kits also include ear and hand warmers, “the first two areas to get cold,” she says. Most costumes are also made loose enough so that the paraders can layer up underneath.

There are roughly 3,500 costumes produced for the balloon handler brigade.

Balloon handlers get a different treatment. “Their costumes are a lot simpler because they have to pay attention to what they're doing,” she says. In fact, some balloons, like Buzz Lightyear, Sorcerer’s Mickey, and the Minion have nearly 100 people handling them. In total, about 3,500 of the costumes are for balloon handlers. “It’s serious business, so they get a coverall and a tabard that’s color coded with a picture of the character they’re holding.” She points out Toad the mushroom for Mario and an alien planet for Buzz Lightyear. And for the Minions, the team even has little cowboy hats.

Of course there are odes to the past in the costumes too. Some historic costumes have been pulled out of the archives, like an intricate Broadway-quality Mother Goose dress. Others have been given new interpretations, like the original character Harold, who debuted in 1945 as a clown, but had stints as a baseball player (as he was seen in Miracle on 34th Street), fireman, and policeman. For this centennial, there will be 100 Harolds—25 of each iteration—as inflatable costumes (balloons aren’t the only ones that are blown up here!).

Prepping for the big day begin bright and early at 4:30 a.m.

With all this prep, dressing thousands of people then operates like clockwork, as they arrive around 4:30 a.m. at ballrooms around town in their street clothes and exit transformed. For 2.5 hours, shuttles transport them all to the parade start line.

After all the pomp and circumstances are over, Montgomery turns to a new phase of the process: Laundry. “All of this goes in giant piles of whites, darks, and colors. We’ve got to get it laundered and put back in size order.”

And once everything is back in order, they start again on the following year’s parade. “No matter what holiday it is, we always have our finger on the pulse of Thanksgiving,” Wright says.

#6135. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6133. How We Pulled It Off: A Pakistani Wedding Under the Mudéjar Arches of Seville

An incredible love story deserves an incredible wedding. Growing up in the Atlanta suburbs, Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a field trip in middle school, then became best friends as teenagers. It was toward the end of high school that their connection turned romantic.

“She got into college and was moving out of state, and it felt like this might be the last chance that I would possibly have to be with this girl,” Awaez remembered. “We decided to see where things would take us.”

Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a middle-school field trip.

The two grew up in the Atlanta area and got together toward the end of high school.

The relationship took them into their twenties through to a proposal in July 2023: an elaborate scavenger hunt that Awaez staged around Chicago, where they lived briefly before turning to Atlanta. When plotting their wedding, they were sure they wanted something just as detailed and thoughtful, and immediately landed on a destination celebration. “We knew we didn’t want to have it in Atlanta, because we didn’t feel like we would be able to give our guests the kind of intentional experience we really wanted to,” says Falaknaz.

Ahead, the couple explains how and why they chose to hold a Seville destination wedding in August 2025 for 160 guests, and discusses the (many!) venues they booked for their various events, the fun guest surprise they plotted, and loads of other sangria-soaked details.

Hotel Alfonso XIII is an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for the Spanish king.

The property and Sevilla in general are known for the Mudéjar-style architecture of Southern Spain.

Falaknaz and Awaez were open to getting married anywhere, a wonderful but intimidating prospect. They scoured Pinterest and spoke to planners across the US. “We looked into Chicago, we looked into California, and at one point we looked into a cabin wedding in Montana,” the bride says. “None of those really felt right until I came across some of the venues in Seville, Spain.”

Her major moment of connection was seeing the Hotel Alfonso XIII, an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for a king of Spain, who aimed to host esteemed international guests there. The scale and vibe of Seville itself—smaller than other European cities, but with an incredible history, stunning architecture, and loads to do—appealed as well. The couple reached out to several planners and booked a trip to visit the Alfonso and several other venues.

In person, the property was just as incredible as they’d hoped. “Hotel Alfonso was honestly a non-negotiable for me once we stayed there that very first trip,” says Awaez. “We were exposed to all the different ways we could utilize the hotel and make the most of it.”

And given the hotel’s 150 rooms, the majority of their guest list could stay there, and did. “One of the major things we wanted from the wedding was everyone to be together. We loved the idea of it being almost a resort, where you’re constantly bumping into people from the wedding,” says Falaknaz.

The couple chose event-planning firm Bodas del Sur because it had worked on South Asian weddings before.

As they tried to narrow down the location for their wedding, the couple had a few dismaying calls with potential event firms. “We met with a lot of planners, and they had a lot of stipulations right off the bat. They weren't really open to hearing what we wanted out of our wedding,” Falaknaz says. They ultimately opted to work with Bodas del Sur, a Seville-based firm that specializes in destination weddings across Andalusia and gave them utter confidence in their ideas. “From our very first conversation, they just seemed like they were going to make what we wanted happen,” the bride continues. “Whatever we said, they ran with it, like, ‘Okay, these are all the ways we can make it happen.’ That was the most reassuring thing: that we felt heard.”

In addition to their vast experience with Seville venues and vendors, Bodas del Sur had also worked on South Asian weddings in the past, says the bride, “so it gave us a lot of confidence that they knew what they were doing.”

A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

A key aspect of the typical South Asian wedding is that it involves several events, and for the couple’s own Muslim-Pakistani celebration, they figured out quickly that not all of them made sense for the Hotel Alfonso XIII. Though Falaknaz began to panic at the realization—“Of course I was like, all hope is lost, we have to go back to the drawing board”—the Bodas team took them to see more spaces, which cemented Seville for them as a whole.

“The first venue they took us to was Casa de Pilatos. We both walked in and were like, ‘Oh my gosh, this is it. We can’t possibly give this up,’” Falaknaz says. “And the more places they took us to, the more we fell in love with Seville.” The biggest draw for the couple was the city’s rich Islamic heritage—it was under Muslim rule for over 500 years—and the corresponding architectural features, such as the arches, pillars, and intricate tiles, a fusion with Christian motifs known as Mudéjar style.

A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th century formerly private home known for its iconic Sevillian architecture.

“That blend was something we just weren’t finding elsewhere,” says Falaknaz. “That’s truly where we felt like we could give our guests the kind of experience we wanted—that would make them feel connected to something that was more than just a wedding.”

The couple held four major events over three days. The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th-century formerly private home commissioned by a nobleman that stands as an apex of Sevillian Romantic architecture. The pithi, another daytime party during which the couple is decorated with turmeric paste to represent a pre-wedding cleansing as well as the golden joy to come, was staged at Hotel Alfonso XIII. The night of dancing and performances, also known as the sangeet, happened at Casa de Pilatos, while the slightly more Western-style wedding reception and its after-party were at Hacienda La Soledad, an estate constructed in 1542 as the center of an olive grove.

The Sevilla celebration of 160 people felt “tiny” compared to the Atlanta nuptials the couple held for their legal ceremony.

The one ceremony the couple didn’t have on site in Spain? The actual wedding itself. Their Nikkah, the Islamic wedding rites, was held at an Ismaili Jamatkhana at home in Atlanta, in an effort to include the much larger guest list of everyone important to their families, about 600 people in all. That contributed to the relatively tiny group of 160 in Seville feeling much more intimate—“Well, intimate was still about 160, but intimate for us,” says Falaknaz.

“We felt connected to doing that in a place where we both grew up. We were able to do it in our mosque at home, the one we grew up going to and where all of our friends and parents’ community is. It was really special to have that be a part of the storyline, that we’ll share hopefully when we have kids,” says Falaknaz. “It was nice to be able to share that with everyone that wouldn't be able to make it to Spain.”

The wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender cala lilies and pearl chandeliers.

Given the spectacular aesthetics of their chosen venues, the couple decided to bring in very little outside decor, and keep what they did bring in complementary. “The intention was to find places that spoke for themselves,” says Awaez. “We wouldn’t have to dedicate so much time to constructing the decor, versus the place standing on its own.”

For their first two events, they matched the color schemes to the major activities, with the pithi blanketed in shades of turmeric (from fluffy roses to mirrored pillows), and the mehendi outfitted in reddish browns and burnt orange. To create the feeling of intimacy and home at the latter, tables and other furniture were kept low, and wide cushions lay on a floor covered in overlapping rugs to encourage lounging.

Their sangeet was a night filled with dance performances, channeling a peacock theme to echo the jewel-toned florals and vivid garden colors.

Their sangeet, the night filled with dance performances, fittingly received a peacock theme, which carried from the feathers embroidered on Falaknaz’s gold gown by Taali to the signage to a jewel-toned palette for the florals. “We pulled colors that we felt would balance the venue, with these beautiful blues in the tiling and obviously the greens in the gardens,” says Falaknaz, who changed into a glittering indigo lehenga by Seema Gujral for her own performance.

The wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender calla lilies and pearl chandeliers, with architectural floral sculptures set around a fountain. Their planners were the key minds behind the creative vibe of the wedding, along with a local florist, La Galería by Jesús Fuertes.

Transportation to the sangeet was by horse-drawn carriage, and the couple's photography sessions included a ride around Seville's iconic Plaza de España.

While the schedule (and culture) of the wedding events was very expected, the couple kept guests on their toes when it came to transportation to the sangeet: They were taken by horse-drawn carriages to Casa de Palatos. “They were so surprised to see a whole bunch of carriages waiting outside for us. It was such a cool moment,” says Awaez. The rides took a scenic route through the Plaza de España before reaching the venue. “We knew that our guests probably weren't going to be able to have a lot of downtime between the events to explore the city,” says Falaknaz of the bonus tour.

Falaknaz wore a glittering lehenga by Seema Gujral.

While much of dinner was Desi dishes, the couple also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella.

A key part of Awaez and Falaknaz’s three planning trips to Seville involved considering the caterers that their planners suggested. “We were genuinely concerned about how the food was going to taste, especially out in Spain in comparison to our typical Indian-Pakistani restaurants here in the U.S.,” says Awaez. “We tested and tried a lot of those options that they shared with us, and found several of our own, and ultimately the two that we landed on were fantastic.” They worked with the staff of the Indian restaurant Taj Mahal Sevilla to cater their sangeet, and Ágape 360 Catering y Eventos for their mehendi and reception.

The gastronomic director of Ágape 360, Manuel de Pablo Deco, is Spanish but was excited to learn and adapt to the couple’s cultural needs: For a few crucial dishes, among them Desi-style karahi paneer and a nihari beef stew, the couple’s mothers actually found YouTube videos demonstrating the technique for cooking the recipes. “We sent those videos over to Manu, and he studied them to a T. He really learned to cook Indian food from scratch,” says the grateful bride.

After days of distinctly Pakistani events, the couple’s wedding reception was an unabashed celebration of the local culture. Tinto de verano, a popular summery version of sangria, was served at the cocktail hour, while passed hors d’oeuvres included tapas bites like torta de potatas, Moorish-spiced meat skewers, and chicken croquettes. A troupe of flamenco dancers performed; the couple had seen the group dance at a taverna their planners had recommended on their first planning trip to Seville. While much of their dinner was Desi dishes, they also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella, in both seafood and vegetarian styles—followed by flan for dessert.

To create the feeling of intimacy, tables and florals were kept low.

A step and repeat served as a photo op for guests to snap their own shots.

To maximize their booking and the guest experience alike, Falaknaz and Awaez utilized each possible room or space within their venues. For the sangeet, they took family and couple portraits in the gardens of the Casa de Pilatos, moved to the central, most ornate courtyard for dinner and speeches, held performances in the soaring “courtyard of the halt,” and then moved to an entirely inner room for the after-party, given the local ordinance in the city center that required outdoor spaces to quiet down after 11:00 pm.

In order to keep the energy high for that final transition, they enlisted the help of their bridal party, who performed the final dance act of the night. “Almost flash mob style, we ran off the stage and through the crowd and into the indoor space,” says Falaknaz. The same crowd-pleasing song that’d been playing outside was already being piped indoors— “Dholi Taro Dhol Baaje,” from the beloved Bollywood movie Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam—so the group of 100+ party-goers was enticed to stay a little longer. Or a lot longer: The party continued back at the hotel’s basement, stretching until 3:00 am.

The couple invited friends to join them after the wedding for a trip to La Tomatina in Valencia.

The end of the trip afforded more one-on-one time with guests than the busy wedding weekend.

Wedding events took place Friday through Monday, and most guests left on Tuesday, though plenty decided to extend their trip on either end. The newlyweds themselves decided to attend La Tomatina festival in Valencia, in which festival-goers eat but also pelt each other with tomatoes—otherwise known as the biggest food fight in the world. They threw out an invitation for any interested guests to join them, and more than 30 wound up attending.

“It was really special to be able to decompress after the wedding with so many of our friends, and actually have more quality time with them than we did at the wedding,” says Falaknaz. And it turned out to be a suitably colorful ending for an unforgettable wedding celebration.

#6132. Norse Atlantic Says Financial Situation ‘Critical’

After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways said Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.

The Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the months since the war started, the airline has cut staff, furloughed some crew members, suspended unprofitable routes, and instituted temporary pay reductions for some non-flying crew, but these steps have apparently not put Norse Atlantic back on solid ground.

“[The company’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials said in a statement. “Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover.”

“Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution,” the message continued. “Norse will provide further information as and when appropriate.”

Rising fuel costs have set back airlines around the world, but the squeeze is arguably worst in Europe, since the continent depends mainly on Gulf oil and has little domestic refining capacity. The crisis has forced Latvia’s airBaltic into bankruptcy, teed up EasyJet’s sale to Apollo Global Management, and inflicted considerable damage on Lufthansa’s core brand.

It was not immediately clear if Norse Atlantic has any candidates in mind for a potential merger. The carrier is not part of any global airline alliance, though it partners with operators such as EasyJet, Norwegian Air Shuttle, and Pegasus through its Norse Connections program.

Bloomberg reported in 2023 and 2024 that the carrier was weighing alliances with larger airlines, possibly through an equity stake, but none were named.

Norse Atlantic operates only long-haul flights. Its network has been adjusted multiple times over the last year in an effort to reduce costs.

#6131. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

There is a lot to love about JetBlue. The airline offers generous legroom, tasty snacks and free Wi-Fi. It also has a fairly straightforward loyalty program.

JetBlue TrueBlue points are easy to earn through flights, partner activity, cobranded credit cards and transferable rewards. They are also easy to redeem because any seat on a JetBlue-operated flight can be booked with points, and there are no blackout dates. The program has become more useful through an expanding network of airline partners, including the Blue Sky partnership with United Airlines.

Here is everything you need to know about the JetBlue TrueBlue loyalty program.

JetBlue serves more than 100 destinations throughout the U.S., Latin America, Canada, the Caribbean and Europe. The airline isn’t part of any global alliance but has a growing roster of airline partners.

With JetBlue being one of the youngest major airlines in the U.S., the TrueBlue loyalty program is a relative newcomer to the points and miles world. The program is revenue-based, so earning and redeeming points are typically tied to ticket prices. However, there are also many ways to earn JetBlue points without even getting on an airplane.

TrueBlue points do not expire. Points Pooling also lets between two and seven friends or family members combine their balances, although members must contribute all of their points to the pool while participating.

Related: How to change or cancel a JetBlue flight

JetBlue isn't part of a global alliance, but TrueBlue members can earn and redeem points with the following airline partners.

JetBlue says earning and redeeming with Cape Air are temporarily unavailable while it updates its systems.

Blue Sky lets TrueBlue members earn points and Tiles on eligible United-operated flights booked through JetBlue and redeem TrueBlue points for United flights through JetBlue. Mosaic members also receive reciprocal perks on United, including priority boarding, one complimentary checked bag, preferred seating and Economy Plus seats at check-in. Base fares receive the above benefits except seat selection, and the partnership does not provide reciprocal lounge access.

You can join TrueBlue for free online, starting at the “basic” level. The four published tiers of JetBlue elite status are:

JetBlue uses Tiles to track progress toward "Perks You Pick" — a selection of benefits you can choose from after earning a set number of Tiles — and Mosaic status. You earn 1 Tile for every:

Government-imposed taxes, government-imposed fees and travel insurance do not earn Tiles. Tiles are a status metric and cannot be redeemed for travel.

This means you could earn elite status entirely through credit card spending, through qualifying travel spending or with a combination of the two.

Before reaching Mosaic 1, members can choose a different Perks You Pick benefit at 10, 20, 30 and 40 Tiles. Through Jan. 31, 2027, the choices include early boarding, priority security, a complimentary first inflight alcoholic drink, double points per dollar spent on a JetBlue Vacations package or 5,000 bonus points.

You can pick each of these only once, even if you earn all four Tile amounts.

Related: JetBlue changes its boarding order with new groups

Mosaic members also choose one Perks You Pick benefit at each status level. Current choices include a pet fee waiver, IHG One Rewards Platinum Elite status, Mint Suite selection priority, FoundersCard Blue membership, a $99 statement credit for an eligible JetBlue credit card, a 20-Tile bonus for the member or another TrueBlue member and 15,000 bonus points.

Changes are coming in 2027: Beginning Feb. 1, members will receive a new tier-specific Perks You Pick menu at each Mosaic milestone, may select the same perk again at a later milestone and will have 60 days to make each choice. A pet fee waiver will become an automatic Mosaic 2 benefit, while eligible JetBlue Premier Card members will gain additional card-exclusive choices.

The information for the JetBlue Premier Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Separately, when BlueFirst service begins Dec. 8, all Mosaic members and one companion on the same reservation will be eligible for complimentary, space-available upgrades on eligible BlueFirst flights. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares will not be eligible.

Related: JetBlue announces first-class upgrades and new elite benefits for 2027

There are many ways to save up for a JetBlue award ticket.

When flying JetBlue, you’ll earn TrueBlue points based on the ticket cost, the fare type and whether you book directly with JetBlue.

JetBlue now sells Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst and Mint experiences, with Base and Flex variants available in most cabins. Base fares earn 1 base point per dollar spent, plus 1 point per dollar when booked on jetblue.com or through the JetBlue app. Standard and Flex fares earn 3 base points per dollar spent, plus 3 points per dollar when booked directly.

You can earn TrueBlue points on eligible flights operated by United Airlines, Condor, Etihad Airways, Icelandair, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines and South African Airways.

United is different from JetBlue's other partners. TrueBlue members earn 5 points per dollar spent on eligible United-operated flights booked through JetBlue; government-imposed taxes, fees and surcharges are excluded. Eligible United flights credited to TrueBlue also earn Tiles. For most other partners, earning depends on the operating airline, the booking class and the distance flown.

You can find each partner’s earning chart in JetBlue’s partner directory.

There are several ways to earn TrueBlue points without flying:

You can also purchase JetBlue points or pool them with other members.

JetBlue also offers Points On Repeat subscriptions. These provide a set number of TrueBlue points each month. Higher tiers add a flight-earning accelerator, while the top tier also includes a 10% rebate on eligible JetBlue award flights. Compare the subscription cost with the value you expect to receive before enrolling.

JetBlue has four cobranded credit cards, all issued by Barclays:

The information for the JetBlue Premier Card, the JetBlue Plus Card, the JetBlue Card and the JetBlue Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

TrueBlue is also a transfer partner of seven flexible rewards currencies at the following transfer rates:

Related: Credit card transfer partners: Guide to transferring points and miles to airlines and hotels

JetBlue uses a dynamic pricing scheme for its own flights, so redemptions are pretty straightforward. You can redeem points for any seat on any JetBlue-operated flight across its entire route network. The more a flight costs in cash, the more it will cost in points.

According to TPG’s November 2026 valuations, TrueBlue points are worth 1.35 cents each on average. To calculate the value of a specific award, subtract any taxes and fees from the cash price, divide the result by the number of points required and multiply by 100. Mint and Cash + Points bookings may offer less value, while some partner awards can offer more.

To check award availability, search for flights on JetBlue’s website as you normally would and check the “Use TrueBlue points” option at the top of the search box. Base fares can now be booked with points, although JetBlue charges $150 per person to change or cancel a Base award.

Cash + Points bookings start at 500 points and are available for JetBlue-operated flights and eligible JetBlue Vacations packages. This option can be useful if you are short on points, but it often delivers less value than a standard award. Cash + Points bookings are not available for partner airline awards.

TrueBlue points can also cover certain seat assignments, checked bags, pet fees and priority security. You can redeem points through TrueBlue Travel for eligible hotel stays and car rentals as well.

In addition to using your points for JetBlue flights, you can redeem TrueBlue points on JetBlue's site for eligible flights operated by United Airlines, Condor, Etihad Airways, Icelandair, Qatar Airways and China Airlines. Cape Air redemptions are temporarily paused.

Partner award availability can be limited, and each one-way award must be operated by a single carrier. Frustratingly, you cannot combine a JetBlue flight and a partner flight on the same one-way award, although you can book the outbound and return on different airlines.

A Points Pooling account can have two to seven members and must include at least one person age 21 or older. Members contribute 100% of the points they earn after joining. The pool leader and anyone granted redemption privileges can use pooled points without the other members' permission, so only pool with people you trust. A member who leaves takes their remaining points balance with them.

Related: Family points pooling: How to transfer and maximize your rewards

While you’re unlikely to get incredible value from your points, the JetBlue TrueBlue program is still useful for many travelers. TrueBlue points are among the easiest domestic airline points to earn and redeem. JetBlue-operated awards do not require an award chart and have no blackout dates, though partner award availability can be restricted.

JetBlue's expanded partner network makes TrueBlue more globally useful. New transfer partnerships with Rove and Bilt also make it easier to top up a balance. JetBlue's revenue-based pricing usually limits the opportunity for exceptional value on its own flights, but straightforward redemptions and occasional high-value partner awards make TrueBlue worth understanding.

#6127. Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call)

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”

As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”
