#6126. This Cruise Proves the Congo is No Heart of Darkness—Or Viral Fad

Occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward. Few places exert quite this pull like the Congo Basin, a thick block of forest and rivers covering much of Central Africa, home to some 150 ethnic groups, and a raft of extraordinary biodiversity. Despite its size and its importance as a counterbalance to climate change, the region endures a dearth of scientific research funding and conservation efforts. Roughly the size of India, it has inspired and vexed many visitors (even those who might otherwise have claimed to have conquered it).

A floating village in the Congo River Basin

The idea could be said to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory. The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley, the first to leave a detailed record of his journey across the Basin, claimed that even after a three-year trek (1874-77) it remained “a region of fable and mystery.” That was exactly the mix sought by Polish sailor Józef Korzeniowski, who, as a boy, looked at the map of Africa, then a white space, and “declared that some day I would go there.” Eventually, and not long after Stanley, he did, and with the captaincy of a steamboat on the Congo River, was tasked with collecting one Mr. Klein, an upcountry agent employed by the brutal Belgian trading company. Korzeniowski was horrified by what he saw along the river—colonization and resource extraction at its cruelest and bloodiest—calling it “the vilest scramble for loot that ever disfigured the history of human conscience and geographical exploration.” Later, Józef Korzeniowski became Joseph Conrad, Mr. Klein became Mr. Kurtz, and the rest is literary history.

Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”

The latest journeyman to apply themself to the region is another Welshman, Ash Dykes, whose TikTok videos of his journey paddling down the Sangha River (a tributary of the mighty Congo River) have received millions of views. By mid-October, Dykes, who calls himself an extreme athlete, was midway through the 400 miles he hoped to cover. His videos—the anxiety and speculation of his preparation; the amplification of the danger en route—are over-exaggerated, designed to amuse his audience; they are spectacle. Looking bewildered in his state-of-the-art inflatable boat, Dykes is most often met by competent, unaffected locals, paddling their wooden pirogues with balletic grace. And brave though Dykes certainly is, most of what he has accomplished—attending a hunt with the Ba’aka people, seeing the forest elephants in Dzanga Baï, or tracking Western lowland gorillas—can be done by just about anyone.

The Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions, is the basin's only passenger cruise.

I, too, was one enchanted by the inscrutability of the Congo Basin, and I dreamt of one day traveling along its rivers and into its forests; in my mind’s eye, I envisioned dusk slipping into night, to the rhythm of a pounding drumbeat. Not long ago, I departed Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, aboard the Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions. As the only such passenger vessel in the Congo Basin, the crew of the Ngalessa is accustomed to receiving rarefied looks from the riverbank. But just as often, the ship’s approach was greeted with aplomb, for it was an event in the villages and brought goods, along with community support and news from away.

In comparison to the coarse and crowded daka-dakas—flat-topped river barges, stuffed with goods and spewing black, acrid smoke as they chunter between Kinshasa and Kisangani—those of us onboard the Ngalessa traveled in glorious comfort: air-conditioning, three square meals a day, and private bathrooms. We also had the benefit of our local guides and their familiarity with the languages, customs, and faces up and down the river. This included, in the riverside village of Ngabe, the appearance of an Ejengi, a forest spirit made of palm fronds that danced and spun as a crowd of onlookers sang, drummed, and screamed in delight.

“Don’t worry,” our guide said. “Look at his dusty bare feet!” Elsewhere, we watched an Indigenous Luma woman cut, strip, and chew twigs into a pulp that could be used as medicinal pain relief. On other days, we kayaked through the flooded forests of the Alima River, and traded with fishermen who brought their slim pirogues against our mammoth ship to hand over smoked fish and fruit.

Kayaking through the flooded forests of the Alima River.

Eight days and 600 miles after leaving Brazzaville, we arrived at the outpost of Ouesso on the Sangha River. I journeyed further upon that water by launch boat, into the Central African Republic, and spent days at Sangha Lodge, drinking gin and tonics with local legend Rod Cassidy, an eco-tourism pioneer who has spent years living and working with the local Ba’aka people. It was through him I had the good luck to attend a hunt with those same Ba’aka, and to look on while they divvied up the duiker they snagged in their homemade nets. Afterwards, they whooped and hollered as they carried the meat out and into their village—a feast!

In the heightened state of travel, there comes occasionally a moment like falling into an empty space and, as two glancing stones can spark a blaze, a light of comprehension is illuminated. Sometimes this moment manifests itself as love, other times as admiration, or confusion. Conrad left the Congo in spiritual, psychological, and physical shock. “Before the Congo, I was a mere animal,” he wrote after his consequential journey. He was changed, as travelers who go forward with their ears and eyes open (to say nothing of their hearts) are changed. Watching the Ba’aka poised in their hunt, ears tilted to the slightest sound, I felt myself see humanity as it had existed since time immemorial. As they laughed and chatted on their success, the women showing their fangs (chipped with rocks as a show of strength), and the men slapping each other on the back, I could barely remember seeing such happiness elsewhere.

The Congo Basin may still be raw and atavistic—great adventures there are still possible—but it is no “heart of darkness” (a title which for Conrad lay not in the location itself, but rather mankind’s ability to exploit and vilify others). What separates it from other places is its independence. It requires protection, yes, but has no need, and few provisions, for any prying visitors; it is not a prize to be conquered. Most incredibly, it remains the home of peoples who have not yet latched themselves to tourism; people who sustain themselves almost wholly from an expanse of forest and the waters that for others can only be the basis of wonder and amazement. And yet, after all the sorrow and misery that colonialism brought to the Congo Basin, the people remain sincere and earnest, and willing to show others the best of their land.

A lone kayaker glides underneath a hazy sky.

One night, as the Ngalessa drifted northward, from beneath the awning on the ship’s upper deck, I watched a cloud bank clump and darken. Finally, with an incision of lightning, the downpour came, brief but fierce. The sun returned, low in the sky but still warm, and the scent of damp earth rose up. A patter of drumming reached us from somewhere, before being swallowed by the forest. The dinner bell rang, and I thought I never want this trip to end.

The United States need not wait for a nuclear attack before acting against a grave danger. But it cannot ask Americans to support an open-ended war on the strength of a danger alone. After more than eight months of conflict with Iran, the Trump administration owes the country a public account of what its campaign has achieved, what remains beyond its ability to verify, and what further fighting would accomplish. The case for preventing an Iranian bomb is strong. The case for continuing this war depends on whether continued force can achieve that end.

#6124. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

#6123. The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

Picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful.

Barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island.

Grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.)

The kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here.

A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable.

Definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants.

If you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind.

There are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling.

The longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights.

A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi.

The rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest.

While Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

One of the top premium cards, the offers many lifestyle-centered benefits and statement credits. Those include several health- and fitness-centered benefits, including an Oura Ring statement credit for up to $200 per calendar year (enrollment is required).

With the end of the calendar year fast approaching, now's a good time to decide whether you can use this credit before it resets.

Here's how this statement credit works and whether it makes sense for you.

One of the many lifestyle statement credits available through the is up to $200 each calendar year toward Oura Ring. Specifically, the statement credit applies to hardware purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. (Enrollment is required.)

The Oura Ring is a wearable, health-tracking smart ring. Some key data it tracks includes:

Imagine an Apple Watch or Fitbit, but in ring form. Oura currently sells the Oura Ring 4 starting at $349 and the newer Oura Ring 5 starting at $399. While this statement credit won't fully cover the cost of a ring, it will get you more than halfway there.

One notable advantage of the Oura Ring is that you don't have to charge it as often as other wearables — the Oura Ring 5 typically lasts six or more days on a full charge.

Related: The best credit cards to maximize fitness spending

Amex states that the statement credit should post within eight weeks, but some TPG staffers have seen it post within days.

If you're trying to use this statement credit before Dec. 31, don't wait for the last minute. Amex relies on the date Oura processes the transaction, which might be a day or two after you place the order.

This is particularly important if you order a sizing kit: The ring itself won't process and ship until you confirm your size in your Oura account. Place your order now to get things started.

Related: Why the new Amex Platinum changes are converting me to a cardmember

This statement credit is a more niche perk that not all cardmembers will be able to use. For starters, many people may prefer other forms of wearables. If health data doesn't interest you, this statement credit won't move the needle either.

Plus, the fact that this statement credit doesn't cover the full cost of the ring may also deter some cardmembers. The out-of-pocket cost will still run you at least $149, unless you land a good sale. You'll also need to pay for an Oura Membership at $5.99 monthly or $69.99 per year.

I hope Amex expands this statement credit to cover a subscription in the future, since it's needed to fully maximize your Oura Ring's features.

Even if Oura Ring is of interest, you may not want to buy a new one every year, meaning some years the benefit may go unused.

If you don't think you’d use the statement credit yourself, you could gift a ring to one of your health- and fitness-minded friends or family members.

It's also important to note that this is a shared statement credit, meaning authorized users do not receive their own.

This sole statement credit shouldn't be the deciding factor on whether you add this card to your wallet, but if you can use it organically, it can help recoup some of the Platinum's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Related: Complete guide to authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card

The Oura Ring statement credit can be valuable for Platinum Card members who already plan to buy a fitness tracker, especially if they can stack it with a sale. However, you might find it smarter to let the statement credit go unused some or all years.

However, it would be ideal if this statement credit were expanded in the future to cover the subscription cost, as this would make it more accessible for more cardmembers to use year after year.

#6120. China Southern Orders 50 737 MAX Jets

A subsidiary of China Southern Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, Reuters reported Tuesday.

The airplanes, which have a total list price of $7.4 billion, will be used by Xiamen Airlines, which is based in Fujian. Deliveries are expected from 2031 to 2034.

The deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade. The country largely shifted toward Airbus aircraft as relations with the U.S. frayed.

President Donald Trump hoped to reverse that trend during his state visit to China in May. Trump discussed a potential purchase directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and even brought along Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg for the summit. Ultimately, Beijing agreed to buy 200 aircraft from Boeing, fewer than analysts expected, but still notable considering Boeing’s drought in the country.

Trump said earlier this week that he thinks China will buy 250 more aircraft from Boeing. He did not provide details or say where that information came from.

China Southern said the new aircraft will help Xiamen expand after it relocates to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport. The facility will replace Xiamen Gaoqi International Airport as Xiamen’s main gateway.

It has been a messy few weeks for air travel in the U.S., and unfortunately, it appears the Thanksgiving rush could bring another big wave of flight delays.

Storm systems developing along both coasts threaten to disrupt holiday plans for travelers catching last-minute flights, though few major problems have been reported (so far). Fewer than 50 Wednesday flights had been canceled as of 1:30 p.m. EST, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware. About 2,800 were delayed, a manageable number for the day's busy holiday light schedule.

However, about 50 of Thursday's flights had been preeemptively canceled — the bulk coming at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) — ahead of a strong coastal storm expected to arrive to the region in the morning. That could foretell bigger problems coming to the Northeast, where travelers scheduled to fly should keep an eye on their flight status.

More broadly, the nation's four biggest airlines had rolled out weather-related rebooking policies for airports facing poor conditions. (Details below.)

On the West Coast, heavy rain and wind are forecast to move into the Pacific Northwest just as travel peaks on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, forecasters are warning of a “monster” storm that could disrupt flights at several of the nation’s busiest East Coast hubs on Wednesday and Thursday.

Further, a new round of storms in South Florida and possible wintry weather in St. Louis added to the mix.

“The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen told TPG.

It’s looking like the latest in a series of frustrations for flyers. In the past two weeks alone, travelers dealt with a nationwide ground stop that led to 18,000 flight cancellations as well as technology outages at United and Delta Air Lines.

Now, it appears Mother Nature will be the biggest obstacle during one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

The West Coast storm is expected to impact the Thanksgiving getaway, although by 7 a.m. local time on Wednesday, the worst of the rainfall appeared to have passed.

Late Monday, United issued a travel advisory for its San Francisco hub amid concerns that high tides could cause flooding at the airport.

Fortunately, Bay Area leaders are no longer worried about flooding at the airport itself.

In recent days, forecasters had grown concerned that heavy rain and high tides could lead to water covering SFO’s taxiways, which are right next to San Francisco Bay.

“At this moment, we are not expecting flood water to reach onto the tarmac at SFO, which is a positive development,” San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said in a social media post — while warning that ground stops because of weather conditions were “still a possibility.”

In a statement to TPG on Tuesday, SFO officials said the airport was keeping pump stations and drainage areas clear, and staging sandbags ahead of the forecast bad weather.

A storm system moves into Washington and Oregon on Wednesday, with locally heavy rain forecast for areas around both Portland and Seattle.

That storm is forecast to last through at least Friday, and although airlines have not issued travel waivers — suggesting they don't expect the storm to be too impactful on their operations — it would still be wise to anticipate possible delays if you're traveling.

The worst travel disruptions, however, could come from a powerful coastal storm developing in the east, meteorologists warn.

That East Coast system could bring strong winds, heavy rain and flooding to a large swath of the coast — including many of the nation’s busiest airports, according to Van Dillen.

He laid out which airports could be heavily affected:

“My advice would be, the earlier you can get to your destination, the better,” Van Dillen advised East Coast travelers.

As of Wednesday morning, the storm was affecting much of the Southeast with locally heavy rain, according to The Weather Channel.

But on Thursday and into Thursday night, the storm is expected to move up to the Northeast, with heavy rain, strong winds and possibly freezing in some areas.

The remnants of the storm could cause lasting delays into Friday, before it peters out by Saturday.

We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

All of the major airlines are offering travel waivers for those flying to, from or through Northeast airports on Thursday, so you may want to consider taking advantage of that if your plans allow.

While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself is typically one of the quietest days of the year at airports.

All eyes will be on how Mother Nature cooperates on Saturday and Sunday, as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

More 2026 Thanksgiving travel coverage from TPG:

Here are some things you should do if you're planning to fly in the next few days.

Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

Take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

Just keep in mind: As more and more cities are affected by bad weather, disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

Have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:

Want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance plan for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.

#6118. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

This is one of the best times of the year to find flight deals. Black Friday is almost here, followed quickly by Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday. All the major airlines, hotels and booking platforms have big sales. Of course, TPG will have roundups of all the best deals, but there are other ways to find deals that I've been experimenting with: artificial intelligence.

I've been an AI skeptic the past few years, at least when it comes to finding and booking travel deals, but it has come a long way since TPG tried to use AI to plan an itinerary back in 2023. (Spoiler: It didn't do a great job.)

But the technology has improved significantly over the past few years, especially when it comes to confirming you are getting a good deal.

ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and Google Gemini can now also help you compare prices and find cheaper airports or travel dates, decipher fare rules and restrictions, and even let you know whether it's better to pay cash or use points or miles.

I still don't find AI great at finding mileage or points awards, but it can do a lot.

"AI is already a powerful tool for finding flight deals and only getting better, but it’s still got a long way to go," Thrifty Traveler executive editor Kyle Potter said. "It’s prone to mistakes and falls victim to phantom award availability."

Still, combining AI with tools like Google Flights and Points Path can make finding deals easier and potentially save you some serious money (or miles).

So it can be a useful tool, but I don’t think it’ll ever be the only tool travelers need.

Here are some ways to use AI to find deals.

Like I always tell people looking for deals, flexibility is key. Rather than asking for a specific date or flight, describe your budget, home airport, ideal travel dates and how flexible you are in your AI tool.

AI will work with tools like Google Flights to help you find a good deal. Here's a sample prompt:

"I'm looking for Black Friday flight deals departing from New York City. My budget is $500 round-trip, I'm flexible on destinations, and I can travel between January and March 2027. Suggest 10 destinations worth checking, including nearby airports and typical fare ranges. Don't invent live prices."

ChatGPT gave me a list of potential deals.

It also showed some of its top picks, including San Juan and Barcelona.

As I continued scrolling, ChatGPT eventually showed me a link to Google Flights Explore, one of my absolute favorite tools for finding flight deals. As you can see, this prompt pulls up a Google Flights search for some cheap trips from New York City-area airports to places nearby and, if you scroll the map, far away, too. I had to narrow the search a bit for just trips in January, but there were a ton of options.

You may be asking yourself why you need AI if you are going to Google Flights Explore anyway. Great point — I think the idea is that ChatGPT can give you a few ideas tailored to your specific interests and budget.

AI can also help you find savings by flying into cheaper airports or on different travel dates that will save you some cash. You might try Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) instead of San Francisco International Airport (SFO), for example. Or, further afield, maybe flying into Brussels and taking a train instead of flying directly into Paris can save you money.

"I want to fly from New York to Paris in February 2027. What nearby departure and arrival airports should I compare? Suggest flexible travel dates and explain which alternative airports have reasonable ground transportation."

ChatGPT suggested a few alternate airports for me in Europe.

Of course, that doesn't really help without seeing the prices. But it will give you some more ideas; you can then check the live prices at Google Flights. Here's where it gets more interesting, though. When I kept pushing the AI tool to find actual deals, it gave me a list of fares to various cities, including Frankfurt and Amsterdam. And when I prodded it again with the prompt, "Anything cheaper if I fly straight to Paris?", it found a couple of better deals.

Those are great deals. Just be sure they are actually bookable. In this case, I did not find the same deal on the FrenchBee website or on Google Flights, but I did find it on Icelandair via Expedia (where Chat had directed me).

So in this case, AI was able to find me an actual deal to Paris, though I likely could have found that same deal by starting my search on Google Flights and avoiding multiple steps. Still, I'm a bit flabbergasted that AI has gotten good enough to find actual flight deals.

With Black Friday almost here, this could be among the most useful ways to use AI.

Airlines love advertising discounts of 20%, 30% or even 50%, but those promotions sometimes apply only to base fares, select dates or specific routes.

AI can help readers understand the fine print and calculate their actual savings.

"I'm considering this Black Friday airfare sale. Analyze the terms and conditions, including blackout dates, excluded routes, baggage charges, booking deadlines and whether the discount applies to the base fare or total ticket price. Tell me what I should verify before booking. Here are the terms: [paste sale details]."

For example, Cathay Pacific has a Black Friday deal on now for "round-trip savings from the U.S. to Hong Kong and destinations across Asia, Australia and New Zealand, with 15% to 25% off Economy, 15% to 30% off Premium Economy and 10% off Business."

I tried to find a round-trip fare from Seattle to Hong Kong, which quoted me $2,687 for premium economy. I then asked ChatGPT if it was a good deal using the prompts above.

ChatGPT told me that, essentially, that wasn't a great deal. When I pressed it to find me a better deal, it couldn't. However, it did find an additional coupon I could use: "promotion code US26BF115 for the additional $115 discount and potential 3,000 bonus Asia Miles."

So when you read the TPG guide to the best Black Friday and Cyber Monday, be sure to ask ChatGPT if it's really a good deal.

Remember that a 40% discount on the base fare doesn't necessarily translate into 40% off the total ticket price.

Want to know if you should use cash or points to pay for your flights? Of course, TPG has a great points and miles calculator, but AI can help, too.

Black Friday airfare sales sometimes make paying cash a better deal than redeeming points and miles.

Readers can use AI to calculate the value of their points and compare cash fares against award tickets.

"I found a Black Friday round-trip flight for $450. The same flight costs 35,000 airline miles plus $50 in taxes. Calculate the cents-per-mile value and explain the trade-offs between paying cash and redeeming miles. Assume both tickets offer comparable benefits."

In this hypothetical example, the redemption yields about 1.14 cents per mile, before accounting for any miles earned on a paid ticket.

Here is a link to TPG's latest points and miles valuations, so you can do your own math, too.

As an illustration, I found a round-trip flight on American Airlines from New York City to Madrid in February for $670. Similar flights cost 60,000 plus $52.09 when booked with miles. I asked ChatGPT if it was a good deal. As you can see, based on TPG valuations, ChatGPT tells me to use cash, not miles.

I've found ChatGPT to be extremely useful in telling me whether to spend cash, miles or points on things like hotels and flights.

Related:10 of our favorite travel hacks from very frequent flyers

Despite my best efforts, AI was not able to find me actual deals for specific flights in most cases. AI still works best as a complement to established flight-search tools, not as a replacement.

Here's an example of a search I tried using Claude's AI. While Black Friday hadn't started yet, it had trouble finding any great deals and didn't show anything in real time.

Of course, I've mentioned Google Flights multiple times, as it's likely your best way to find those flight deals.

Another tool that TPG loves is Points Path. Download it to layer on top of Google Flights to flag good deals on points. Points Path can also send you alerts on good award deals.

For the best results, use award search tools like Seats.aero, Roame.travel or Point.me, alongside AI. You can search for business-class availability and even set alerts to be emailed when the award you are looking for opens.

Related: These new tools will track your flights and get you refunds if the price drops

I track my flights with two other new tools. PAiback has given me back $148 this year alone. I've also been experimenting with Junova. Both companies will monitor cash prices and get you refunds if the price drops, charging you a commission on the money saved.

New users at Junova get a $25 credit when signing up through the TPG referral link (so you get a $25 credit — then when you pay the 20% commission, it comes out of your $25 "bank"). We also like Autopilot.

The point of all this is that, in my experience, AI can't yet find good flight or points deals, though I will keep playing with it. My next move is to try to integrate it with one of my flight deal search companies, but we are not there just yet.

As previously mentioned, there is a lot AI still can't do perfectly. Remember that AI can hallucinate fares, routes, promotions and availability. In most cases, AI chatbots have access to live airline pricing; AI tools may present outdated prices or expired deals. AI-generated fare comparisons may also forget taxes, fees or baggage charges. Finally, even if AI finds you a great trip, the itinerary may disappear before you can book it.

And remember, points and miles deals are still very elusive even with the power of artificial intelligence.

As Potter from Thrifty Traveler told me, "In an age when airlines are getting stingier with award space — and there are more savvy travelers redeeming points than ever before — those great award deals are increasingly dynamic, hinging on new routes or airline capacity changes that can appear and vanish within not just hours but minutes."

In other words, AI won't be able to grab you those incredible deals like companies like Thrifty Traveler can.

Always confirm the final price, itinerary and fare rules before purchasing.

As someone who spends a good chunk of every day searching for flight deals, I've been pleasantly surprised by how far artificial intelligence has come. While I'm not ready to give up my favorite flight search tools, AI has earned a place in my travel-planning arsenal.

Whether you're shopping for Black Friday, Cyber Monday or Travel Tuesday deals, AI can help you think outside the box, identify cheaper destinations and alternative airports, decipher complicated sale terms, and determine whether you're better off paying cash or redeeming points and miles.

Just don't take everything AI tells you at face value. I've encountered plenty of fares that I couldn't actually book, and AI still has a long way to go when it comes to finding award availability.

For now, the sweet spot is combining AI with tried-and-true tools like Google Flights, Points Path and flight deal-alert services. And, as always, flexibility remains your greatest asset when looking for cheap flights.

AI may not be the ultimate travel deal finder just yet, but it could help you become a smarter shopper — and save you some serious cash or miles in the process.

#6116. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6114. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Here’s every promotion on purchased IHG Rewards Points we’ve tracked since January 2026, with the cost per point for each, so you can see how the current deal stacks up.

Is this a good deal? At 0.54 cents per point, the current promotion is 50% below the standard price. That matches the best deal we’ve tracked.

Cost per point at the largest purchase tier, including the 7.5% tax. Lower is better.

Every IHG Rewards Club buy points promotion since January 2026

*Cost per point is for the largest purchase tier and includes the 7.5% tax.

Between 12:01 AM ET on November 23 and 11:59PM ET on December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is structured as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status, and purchased points will post within 72 hours of an eligible purchase (though usually much faster than that). Furthermore, the purchase of points is non-refundable.

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses, and that’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 300,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 600,000 points at a cost of $3,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 300,000 points, pre-bonus.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

Do you plan on buying IHG points with a bonus?

#6113. Avianca Adds New U.S. Route

Colombian flag carrier Avianca is adding a new connection to the U.S. Northeast.

Starting Feb. 2, 2027, the airline will offer service between Barranquilla and New York-JFK.

Flights will operate four times weekly using Airbus A320-family aircraft, each with up to 180 seats.

“The launch of this nonstop route to New York reaffirms our commitment to [Barranquilla] and the entire Colombian Caribbean region,” Avianca President Gabriel Oliva said in a statement. “We want to continue connecting regions with major international markets, making travel easier, supporting tourism, and contributing to Colombia’s economic development.”

Avianca currently serves JFK from Bogota, Cartagena, Medellín, Pereira, Colombia, Guatemala City, San Salvador, El Salvador, Quito, and Guayaquil. From Barranquilla, it flies to Miami, Bogota, Medellín, and Cali.

#6112. Air traffic funding turbulence

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy upped the ante on aviation funding after a nationwide ground stop. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

A nationwide ground stop of all flights has intensified a funding battle over air traffic control modernization. #6111. Chase Freedom Unlimited Review: No Annual Fee & 1.5x Points Everywhere

The no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value. The card offers 3% cash back (or 3x points) on dining, 1.5% cash back (or 1.5x points) on everyday spending, and there are ways to get significantly more value than that.

I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right. The catch is that there’s a learning curve to using this card — for some people this will just be a good card, while for other people this will be an amazing card.

This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.

Link: Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®

Before I get into my detailed Chase Freedom Unlimited review, let me summarize some of the basics:

Here are my thoughts on the main Chase Freedom Unlimited pros and cons:

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is part of Chase’s “Freedom” card portfolio, and is an excellent complement to any of Chase’s cards earning Ultimate Rewards points. Before diving into all those details, let’s look at the Freedom Unlimited’s welcome bonus, eligibility, and fees, since those are obviously major factors people consider when applying for cards.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited currently has a welcome bonus whereby you can earn $200 cash back (20,000 points) after spending $500 within the first three months.

On the surface, points can be redeemed for one cent each, but you can potentially get a lot more value than that, as these points can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value those at 1.7 cents each.

It’s worth mentioning that the Chase Freedom Unlimited comes with an introductory APR offer that breaks down into two parts: purchases and balance transfers. Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on purchases, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

For balance transfers: Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on balance transfers, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

These intro APR periods can be useful, but just make sure you pay off your entire balance before the offer ends. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck paying a high interest rate, which defeats the purpose.

Eligibility for the Chase Freedom Unlimited is unrelated to eligibility for any other Chase cards, so you could earn the bonus on this card and the Freedom Flex Card, etc. The Chase Freedom Unlimited is not available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months.

Chase’s general credit card application rules, such as 5/24, generally apply, though that rule isn’t necessarily consistently enforced anymore.

There’s not a published credit score you need to get approved for the Freedom Unlimited, though I’d hope to have a score in the good to excellent range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, which is unbeatable. You can also add authorized users to the card for no fee, so you can accrue rewards for their spending as well as your own. Obviously that’s a major upside of the card.

While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a fantastic card for purchases within the United States, it does have 3% foreign transaction fees, so I don’t recommend using this card abroad.

If you’re looking for a great card with no foreign transaction fees, consider the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) or Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more).

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has an awesome rewards structure, which not only includes an excellent return on everyday spending, but also includes some valuable bonus categories.

Before we get into this, note that in each case the percentage cash back can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points, at a rate of one cent per point. I’ll talk more below about how that’s possible, but that’s really how you maximize value with the card.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 5% cash back on travel purchased through Chase Travel℠ (or potentially 5x Ultimate Rewards points). Purchases made outside the Chase travel portal will earn 1.5% cash back (or 1.5 Ultimate Rewards points per dollar).

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back on dining, including takeout and delivery (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is great for a no annual fee card, as this essentially makes this one of the best credit cards for dining spending.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back at drugstores (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is an awesome bonus, since drugstores isn’t a category where you otherwise see many cards offering bonuses.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday spending (or potentially 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points). The 1.5% cash back return isn’t that exciting, given that other cards offer 2% cash back. What is valuable, however, is the ability to earn 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent, as there’s no better Chase card for everyday spending.

Personally I value Chase points at 1.7 cents each, so to me the card offers the equivalent of a 2.55% return on everyday spending.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday purchases, and 3-5% cash back in select bonus categories. On the surface, those rewards are really straightforward, as you can redeem the cash back for statement credits, a direct deposit in an eligible Chase account, for gift cards, or for travel booked through Chase Travel. You can even redeem your cash back toward Amazon purchases, though at the rate of 0.8 cents per point (so please don’t redeem that way!!).

However, if you’re looking to earn travel rewards, you can get a significantly better return on spending than that.

While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a cash back card, in reality the card earns Ultimate Rewards points. You earn 1.5x points per dollar spent, and then ordinarily each point can be redeemed for one cent cash back. That’s how Chase arrives at the valuation of 1.5% cash back with the card.

However, if you have the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with another card that earns “premium” Ultimate Rewards points, then you can do significantly better. These cards include the following:

With one of those cards, suddenly your points are much more valuable. Transferring points between cards is easy and can be done online. You can learn more about that process in this post.

Personally, the way I like to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is to transfer them to airline and hotel partners, which include the following:

This can be the best way to redeem points toward premium travel experiences. If you want to redeem for first or business class travel or stay at luxury hotels, this option is for you.

One thing worth noting is that Chase recently devalued the transfer ratio to World of Hyatt to 4:3 for the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred. You’ll need the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Reserve for Business to get the full 1:1 transfer rate with Hyatt. No matter which of these cards you have, points transfer to all other partners at a 1:1 ratio.

While my favorite way to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is through the transfer partners, there are also ways to redeem Chase points at an advantageous rate toward travel purchased through Chase Travel℠:

That increases the value of your points by up to 100% right there.

For a no annual fee card, the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers a solid selection of benefits and purchase protection, which cardmembers will certainly appreciate. Let’s cover those, though let me of course remind everyone to always check the guide to benefits for the latest terms & conditions associated with these perks.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you can extend the time period of your United States manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of three years or less. If you’re making an expensive purchase, this could save you a huge amount.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you’re covered for new purchases for 120 days against damage or theft of up to $500 per item, and up to $50,000 per account. Again, this makes the card an excellent option for everyday spending, given how much money purchase protection can save you.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited will reimburse cardmembers up to $1,500 per covered traveler and $6,000 per trip on prepaid fares that can’t be cancelled if your trip is canceled or cut short by sickness or another covered reason. More premium cards have more travel protections and higher limits, but this is pretty nice for a no annual fee cash back card.

With Chase Credit Journey, you get unlimited access to your credit score and more. This is free for Chase customers, including those who have the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money, and having the Chase Freedom Unlimited gives you access to that.

With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you get six months of complimentary DashPass membership. Note that when you take advantage of this, you’ll be auto-enrolled in a paid DoorDash plan after six months, at the rate of $9.99 per month. So you’ll want to be sure you cancel before the complimentary plan expires, assuming you don’t value it.

DoorDash DashPass gets you $0 delivery fees and lower service fees on eligible orders through both the DoorDash and Caviar delivery platforms. You get up to $10 off non-restaurant DoorDash orders each quarter, up to $40 a year. This perk is currently valid for enrollment through December 31, 2027.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited qualifies for 2% cash back on Lyft purchases made through the app — a 0.5% bonus on top of the card’s standard earning rate. This promotion runs through September 30, 2027.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is one of the all around best cards for everyday spending. It’s a credit card that I have, and it’s one that I think is worth holding onto.

If you’re in the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem and put everyday spending on cards in the portfolio, then picking up the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a must. However, the key is to have the card in conjunction with a card earning premium Ultimate Rewards points — the Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Ink Business Preferred, or Sapphire Reserve for Business — so that you’re really maximizing your rewards.

I’d also like to look a bit more closely at the best strategy to take with the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

I can’t emphasize enough that having the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with either the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve is probably the best card combo you can have. That’s because not only can you combine the benefits of the two cards, but this greatly increases the value you get from your Freedom Unlimited points.

For example, if you have the Sapphire Reserve and Freedom Unlimited:

There are currently two Chase Freedom products you can apply for — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and Chase Freedom Flex® Credit Card (learn more). Both cards have no annual fees, so what are the major differences between the cards?

The cards otherwise have overlapping bonus categories, like offering 3x points on dining and drugstores, etc. Personally I think both cards are worth having. If I could just have one, though, I’d probably choose the Freedom Unlimited, since it’s better for everyday spending.

Chase has two “Unlimited” cards — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (learn more). These cards are very similar — both have no annual fee, and both offer 1.5x points (the Ink Unlimited on business purchases). So, what’s the difference?

Other than those differences, the two cards are very similar. I have both of these cards (yes, I have a lot of Chase credit cards).

The Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) is probably the closest competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, regardless of whether you’re looking to earn points or cash back.

The Citi Double Cash also has no annual fee and offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back after you pay for that purchase in the form of ThankYou points. So you’ll earn 2.0 cents back on the dollar, rather than 1.5. Furthermore, in conjunction with a card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) or Citi Strata Elite® Card (learn more), you can move points at the best possible ratio to travel partners.

Since I value Citi ThankYou and Chase Ultimate Rewards points roughly equally, this could also be an attractive card for everyday spending.

The reason some people may still prefer the Freedom Unlimited is because of the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem. On top of that, the Freedom Unlimited has bonus categories, which the Citi Double Cash doesn’t have.

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, and it has a few pros and cons. The Capital One VentureOne has no annual fee and no foreign transaction fees, and offers a minimum of 1.25x miles per dollar spent.

Those miles can either be redeemed for one cent each toward a travel purchase, or they can be moved to Capital One’s airline and hotel transfer partners.

The downside of the VentureOne is that the rewards structure isn’t as lucrative, on the surface. The upside, though, is the lack of foreign transaction fees, and the ability to directly transfer points to airline and hotel partners, even without having another card.

So which card is better depends on whether you’re looking for a “one size fits all” no annual fee card, or want to use it as part of a larger strategy.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited is a key card to maximizing your overall Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, in conjunction with the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, and offers a minimum of 1.5x points per dollar spent. Let me make my advice as concise as possible here: if you have the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, then you absolutely should have the Freedom Unlimited, so you’re maximizing your return on everyday, non-bonused Chase spending.

Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®
