There are all kinds of rewards these days — for travel, dining, retail, or even your local coffee shop.

But there's one currency built specifically for sports fans that rewards you with all the things that drive your fandom — tickets, gear, collectibles and even unique experiences.

And thanks to the new Fanatics American Express® Card, there are now even more opportunities to earn it.

Here’s everything you need to know about FanCash, Fanatics' loyalty currency.

FanCash is the one currency built for sports fans. It takes everything we love about a loyalty program — great earning rates and a variety of redemption options — and merges it with the passion so many of us feel for our favorite sports teams. The end result? The best way to turn your fandom into real rewards.

But now, there are even more ways to earn FanCash, thanks to the launch of the new Fanatics American Express Card. This card takes your fandom to the next level by rewarding you with unlimited 5% FanCash on purchases across the full Fanatics ecosystem. Plus, you can earn 5% FanCash on ticket purchases and select streaming partners.*

Any FanCash you earn will expire one year from the date of purchase. However, any subsequent eligible Fanatics purchase will automatically extend the expiration date for qualifying FanCash in your account.

But with the Fanatics American Express Card, the FanCash earned on the card will never expire, as long as you remain an active cardmember.

You can start earning rewards by signing up for a free Fanatics ONE account.

The best way to earn FanCash is with the new Fanatics American Express Card. For starters, you'll earn unlimited 5% FanCash across the entire Fanatics ecosystem — including Fanatics.com, Lids, Mitchell & Ness, Fanatics Collect, Topps.com, League stores and more. You'll also earn 5% FanCash on tickets from other vendors and select streaming partners, plus 2% FanCash on all other purchases.* And when you stack on the Fanatics App, you can earn 8% or more.

In addition, new cardholders earn $100 FanCash after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 90 days. Plus, earn an additional $100 FanCash for spending $500 a month for 12 consecutive months.**

The Fanatics American Express Card has no annual fee*** and no foreign transaction fees — allowing you to earn a ton of FanCash every year, whether you’re close to home or cheering for your favorite team from abroad.

Finally, eligible U.S. Membership Rewards cardmembers with American Express-issued cards can now transfer Membership Rewards points into FanCash — at a rate of 1,000 points for $10 in FanCash — giving you even more opportunities to spend on gear, collectibles, tickets and more.

Once you’ve earned FanCash, there are a variety of ways to use it across the Fanatics ecosystem. $1 in FanCash gets you $1 in rewards toward your purchase. It’s that simple. No complicated redemption math. That $100 NFL or NBA jersey you've been eyeing? It can be yours for $100 in FanCash.

But perhaps the most powerful aspect of this loyalty currency is that there’s no minimum redemption amount. Unlike other cash-back rewards, you don’t need to wait until you’ve accumulated a certain amount to begin saving — though the more FanCash you have, the more redemption options you unlock.

But it’s the other features of the Fanatics American Express Card that are potentially even more exciting for sports fans.

For starters, cardholders receive 2,500 Fanatics ONE Tier Points upon approval, immediately unlocking Member Pro status and even more rewards and benefits. Plus, you'll receive an additional 2,500 Tier Points every year you have the card.^ This unlocks even more rewards and benefits through the Fanatics ONE program.

Plus, you can select from one of over 500 players for your card design, turning the card itself into a collectible — and a badge of your fandom in your wallet.

Finally, starting in 2027, you’ll have access to the Championship Challenge as a cardholder. If you correctly predict all four champions across the NFL, NBA, NHL, and MLB, you’ll get up to $100,000 of your annual spending back.

Eligibility requirements apply for the Championship Challenge. Program details, including timing and structure, are subject to change. Terms and conditions apply. Full details to be announced prior to launch.

FanCash is the currency designed to reward sports fans for purchases they're already making. And with the new Fanatics American Express Card, plus the ability to convert Amex Membership Rewards points into FanCash, there are more ways than ever to turn your fandom into tangible rewards.

And with even more exciting benefits to come next year, now is the perfect time to join the waitlist and be among the first to know more.

#6109. Park Hyatt Dubai Reopening In 2027, After Full Renovation: First Look At New Rooms

In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation. That was probably good timing, given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.

The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the new room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota. Let’s take a look at those details, but first, I’d like to briefly talk about why I have a soft spot for this property.

Dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points. I don’t have a single favorite hotel in the city, as it really depends on so many factors, from what you’re willing to pay, to the area you want to be in, to how big you want the property to be, to what you value most.

After all, the concept of hotels in Dubai is a bit different than in other cities, given that alcohol is primarily only served at restaurants in hotels. As a result, hotels are very much the social scenes, both for guests and non-guests.

Anyway, the 223-key Park Hyatt Dubai opened all the way back in 2005, and I can’t count how many times I’ve stayed there over the years, going back to just shortly after it initially opened. There’s a lot to like about the resort:

To me, it very much fits into the category of being an urban resort, in terms of being a destination, while having ideal proximity to things.

There are just some hotels where you have such fond memories for a variety of reasons, and for me, the Park Hyatt Dubai is definitely among them. In part, maybe it can’t help but remind me of the “good old days” of redeeming Alaska Mileage Plan miles for Emirates first class.

Remember being able to redeem 100,000 Alaska miles for Emirates first class from the US to basically anywhere in the world via Dubai, with a free stopover there, and no carrier imposed surcharges? And that says nothing of being able to fly from the US to London with a stopover in Mauritius, and layovers in Dubai twice on a one-way (IYKYK). 😉

In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed for the main portion of its renovation. If you go to the hotel’s website, you’ll see the following restrictions:

Park Hyatt Dubai is currently closed as it embarks on a defining transformation – a moment of careful, considered renewal in pursuit of an experience that is more refined, more exceptional, and more authentically itself than ever before.

Behind the scenes, every space and every detail is being thoughtfully elevated – honouring the quality and commitment to luxury hospitality that have made this sanctuary on Dubai Creek so singular, while reimagining the perfect stay.

With an anticipated reopening date of Q1 2027, we look forward to sharing more updates as that moment approaches, and to welcoming you back to a truly reawakened Park Hyatt Dubai. Because true elegance never stands still. It evolves – and in evolving, it is perfected.

As it currently stands, the hotel is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. Now, the hotel is accepting villa reservations as of January 1, 2027, but that’s separate from the main part of the hotel. We’ve known that everything about the hotel would change, but not many renderings had been shared up until now.

One thing is for sure — there’s no denying that the rooms were in desperate need of a renovation, given that they hadn’t undergone any meaningful updates since the hotel first opened.

The hotel has now updated its website to show pictures of the new room product, and you can find those renderings below. I’m conflicted here. On the one hand, this looks much more luxurious than the old setup. On the other hand, the design just looks incredibly generic, and like it could be anywhere. I wish we’d see a little more sense of place.

On the plus side, the hotel’s grounds and general bones otherwise have a decent sense of place, so I hope that’s at least maintained with the updates.

Leadership at the Park Hyatt Dubai had been vocal about how they hope to charge much higher rates after the renovation. I think it’s safe to say that’s all up in the air, based on how the situation in the Middle East evolves. As things currently stand, I see entry level rates in April that are $600+, while I see the lowest rates in summer at $350+.

I feel like that pricing is very much on the optimistic side, but again, there are lots of moving parts with the Middle East hotel situation.

The Park Hyatt Dubai closed in May 2026, and is currently undergoing a full renovation. In recent years we’ve seen a new beach club and new dining outlets added, but this should be by far the most meaningful update since the hotel opened over two decades ago.

The hotel is expected to fully reopen in April 2027, and the new rooms look like a huge improvement in terms of how luxurious they are. However, there’s definitely a sense of place missing, so I’m curious how the overall design evolves.

What do you make of the changes coming to the Park Hyatt Dubai?

#6108. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6107. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an update to reflect that.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-new cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

A post shared by Aeroméxico (@aeromexico)

For those who don’t want to watch the video, below are some screen grabs.

Side note — is this new, or has Aeromexico been doing a cute tequila service for a long time?!? If I knew Aeromexico was serving shots, I would’ve prioritized the airline much higher on my list of products to review. 😉

While details are otherwise limited, we know that Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new seat. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out between 2029 and 2031, so unfortunately patience will be required.

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#6106. New York JFK Terminal 6 Is Almost Open: Airlines & Lounges Moving In

New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is currently undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:

The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

All things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

Roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:

There is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

We know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

Now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

In terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the new lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

The Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s new lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

Are you excited for the new JFK Terminal 6?

Before applying for a Southwest credit card, it's important to understand both Chase's general application restrictions and the rules specific to Southwest cards. These restrictions can affect whether you're approved for a card and whether you're eligible to earn its welcome bonus.

Since Southwest credit cards are issued by Chase, applicants are subject to the issuer's general application restrictions.

Here are a few key rules to keep in mind:

In addition to Chase's general restrictions, Southwest cards have their own rules that can affect your eligibility.

Personal Southwest cards: Chase generally restricts cardholders to one personal Southwest credit card at a time. You also generally won't qualify for another personal Southwest card if you've received a welcome bonus on any personal Southwest card within the past 24 months.

Business Southwest cards: The two Southwest business cards have separate eligibility restrictions. You generally can't qualify for a particular business card if you currently hold that same card or received its welcome bonus within the past 24 months. However, holding one Southwest business card doesn't automatically prevent you from qualifying for the other.

There's no publicly disclosed minimum credit score required to qualify for a Southwest credit card, but applicants generally have the best chances of approval with good to excellent credit — typically a FICO score of 670 or higher.

However, your credit score isn't the only factor Chase considers. Your income, existing debt, credit history and recent credit card applications can also affect your approval odds.

When planning your Southwest card applications, timing and sequence matter. Start by checking your 5/24 status since personal card eligibility depends on the number of new cards you've opened in the past 24 months.

Many travelers start with a business card because these don't trigger the personal card "family" restriction, keeping personal card options open for later.

Business cards also tend to offer strong welcome bonuses and make it easier to split business and personal expenses.

Due to Chase’s application restrictions on personal Southwest cards, it’s a good idea to wait for the highest welcome bonus available or when a Companion Pass is offered before applying.

But remember, Southwest recently announced that its credit card welcome bonuses will soon no longer qualify for earning a Companion Pass. So, if you're hoping to quickly earn a Companion Pass with the help of an eligible Southwest credit card offer, you'll need to apply and be approved for the card by Dec. 2.

#6104. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6103. Capital One Venture Card Bonus: 75K Miles + $300 Credit Welcome Offer (Last Chance)

At the moment, the $95 annual fee Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is offering a phenomenal limited time welcome bonus, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d like to provide an update that this is the last chance to pick up the card with this offer, as it’s expected to be pulled soon.

Not only is this among the best offers we’ve seen on the card, but this is also a reasonably priced travel rewards card that offers long term value, especially for everyday spending.

Link: Learn more about the Capital One Venture Card

The Capital One Venture Card is currently offering a limited time, lucrative, two-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn 75,000 Capital One bonus miles, plus a $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, after spending $4,000 within the first three months.

For context, Capital One miles can be redeemed for a minimum of one cent each, meaning the 75,000 miles will get you at least $750 in value. However, I value the miles at 1.7 cents each based on my latest analysis (see my methodology here), thanks to the value you can get by transferring the miles to travel partners. That means that to me, the 75,000 miles are worth $1,275.

There are lots of great ways to redeem Capital One miles, as they can be transferred to Capital One’s roughly 20 airline and hotel partners. That’s my preferred use of them, as you can get some amazing travel experiences this way.

Partners include programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, and more. These are all programs that allow you to really maximize your points and get outsized value. Just to give a couple of examples of Capital One mileage redemption opportunities:

That doesn’t include the value of the $300 Capital One Travel credit, which posts upon account approval (rather than upon completing minimum spending). The idea is that this can be used for a hotel or vacation rental booking through Capital One Travel in your first cardmember year (in the first 12 months), and it’s valid across one or multiple stays. In other words, you could use it to pay virtually nothing for a $300 hotel stay. All-in-all, I’d say the Capital One Venture bonus is worth up to $1,575.

By my valuation, the current Capital One Venture Card bonus is the best publicly available offer that we’ve seen in over five years, so that makes this the ideal time to apply, and I absolutely wouldn’t wait for a better offer. Quite to the contrary, when this limited time offer gets pulled, it’ll almost certainly be worse.

For context, below is a history of the publicly available bonuses that we’ve seen on the Capital One Venture in recent years.

As you can see, we’ve never seen a publicly available welcome offer of over 75,000 miles, in terms of the mileage component. We have in the past seen $250 travel credits offered along with the miles, and this time around the travel credit is bigger. So offers really don’t get better than this on the card.

When you look at the bonus terms on the Capital One Venture Card, you’ll find the following language:

You are not eligible for this product if you have received a new cardmember bonus for the Capital One Venture card or the Capital One Venture X card in the past 48 months.

As you can see, the card follows a 48-month rule, so you’re not eligible for the welcome bonus on this card if you’ve received a new cardmember bonus on this exact card or on the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) in the past 48 months.

Other than that, eligibility is unrelated to having any other credit card, and Capital One doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for cards.

The Capital One Venture Card has a reasonable $95 annual fee, and offers a variety of perks beyond the excellent welcome bonus:

While the Capital One Venture Card is awesome, how does it compare to the Capital One Venture X Card, which is Capital One’s ultra premium credit card? The Venture X has a $395 annual fee, so the fee is significantly higher, but it also offers several great perks that should more than justify the annual fee. Among other things, the Venture X offers:

So when it comes to the Capital One Venture vs. Venture X, personally I think the Venture X is an even better value than the Venture. However, I know some people just want to avoid higher annual fee cards in general, so for those people, the Venture could be a better option.

The limited time Capital One Venture Card bonus currently offers 75,000 Capital One miles plus a $300 Capital One Travel credit upon completing minimum spending. This Capital One Venture bonus is significantly better than usual, so if you’re eligible for the card based on the 48-month bonus rule, I’d absolutely recommend applying. This is the last chance, as the offer is expected to be pulled soon.

Anyone plan to pick up the Capital One Venture Card with this great bonus?

#6102. Delta Plans Seattle To Singapore A350 Flights, Carrier’s Third Longest Route

We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed plans to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional update, as an announcement about the new route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

Back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

My guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

One certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s new Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

In both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

It’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

It’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

The most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

Delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:

It also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

Delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a new Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

It’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time…

What do you make of Delta’s plans to fly to Singapore?

#6101. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

If you have the (see rates and fees), you may have wondered whether it's worth upgrading to the (see rates and fees).

The Quest comes with a higher $350 annual fee, compared to the Explorer's $150 annual fee ($0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150). But it also offers additional perks, including two free checked bags, $200 in annual United TravelBank cash and a head start toward United elite status.

As a Quest cardholder myself, I think the card can be well worth its annual fee; however, there are a few things I'd consider before upgrading.

Here are five reasons you might want to make the switch — and a few things to consider before you do.

Before deciding whether to upgrade, it helps to see how the two cards stack up. Here's a side-by-side comparison of their key benefits.

Related: Which United credit card is right for you? Comparing the Explorer, Quest, Club and Business cards

If you regularly check bags when flying United, you likely already appreciate the 's complimentary first checked bag for you and a companion on the same reservation.

The takes that benefit a step further, offering both your first and second checked bags free for you and a companion on eligible United-operated flights.

It might not sound like much, but it can lead to substantial savings if you regularly travel with multiple bags.

For example, United's second checked bag can cost up to $60 each way on domestic flights. If you and a companion each check two bags on a round-trip flight, the Quest could save you up to $240 in second-bag fees compared to the Explorer.

That's already more than the $200 difference between the cards' ongoing annual fees.

As a Quest cardholder, I've gotten substantial value from this benefit, since I frequently travel with checked bags. Of course, if you rarely check more than one bag, the Explorer's baggage benefit may be all you need.

Keep in mind that to receive the complimentary checked bag benefits, you generally must include your MileagePlus number in the reservation and purchase your tickets with your eligible United card.

Related: Who should (and shouldn’t) get the United Quest Card?

Sure, the might cost $200 more per year than the after the first cardholder year, but there's one perk that can help make up that difference in one fell swoop: the $200 annual United TravelBank benefit.

Quest cardholders automatically receive $200 in United TravelBank cash after account opening and each year on their account anniversary. These funds can be used toward future eligible flights operated by United or United Express.

Meanwhile, Explorer cardholders can earn $100 in United TravelBank cash after spending $10,000 on purchases in a calendar year.

If you regularly book United flights, the Quest's $200 TravelBank benefit should be relatively easy to use. And if you value the full $200, it effectively brings the card's $350 annual fee down to $150 before factoring in any other benefits.

I've personally found this to be one of the most straightforward Quest benefits to maximize. Since I fly United regularly, I typically put my TravelBank cash toward flights when fares are on the higher side, such as cross-country trips from my home base in San Francisco to Washington, D.C., where I have family.

If you know you'll spend at least $200 on eligible United flights each year, this benefit alone could make a strong case for upgrading to the Quest, especially if you aren't currently earning the Explorer's TravelBank benefit.

If you regularly purchase United flights, upgrading to the Quest could help you earn more MileagePlus miles.

The United Quest earns 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights, compared to 9 total miles per dollar spent with the Explorer. These totals include the 6 miles per dollar spent that general MileagePlus members earn on eligible fares, plus 4 miles per dollar spent from the Quest or 3 miles per dollar from the Explorer.

The Quest also earns 4 miles per dollar spent on other eligible United purchases, compared to 3 miles per dollar spent with the Explorer (mileage earning rates differ for Basic Economy or base-option tickets).

That means you'd earn an additional mile per dollar on eligible United spending by upgrading.

For example, if you spend $3,000 on eligible United purchases in a year, you'd earn 3,000 more miles with the Quest than with the Explorer.

While earning more miles is always nice, I wouldn't recommend upgrading solely for this difference. Unless you're spending a substantial amount with United, the additional miles probably won't justify the $200 difference in ongoing annual fees.

But they're a nice bonus if you're already considering the Quest for its other benefits.

If you're trying to earn United Premier status, the Quest offers a couple of advantages over the Explorer.

Both cards earn 1 Premier qualifying point (PQP) for every $20 spent on purchases. However, the Explorer caps these earnings at 1,000 PQP per calendar year, while the Quest allows you to earn up to 18,000 PQP annually through card spending.

The Quest also provides an annual bonus of 1,000 PQP, awarded within six to eight weeks after Feb. 1 each year. To qualify, your account must be open as of Dec. 31 of the previous year and remain open when the points are awarded.

The annual bonus provides a head start toward Premier status without a spending requirement.

As a United Premier Silver member, I've found the Quest's PQP benefits helpful in working toward maintaining my status.

That said, I wouldn't necessarily recommend putting large amounts of everyday spending on the Quest solely to earn PQP. Depending on your goals, you may get more value from using a card that earns transferable rewards.

Both the Explorer and Quest offer statement credits for purchases like ride-hailing services (activation required), Instacart orders and hotel stays. But the Quest offers higher potential savings in several categories.

For example, the Quest provides up to $100 annually in ride-hailing credits and up to $180 in Instacart credits, compared to $60 and $120, respectively, with the Explorer. Both cards' Instacart benefits are currently scheduled to end Dec. 31, 2027.

The Quest also offers up to $150 in annual credits for eligible Renowned Hotels and Resorts stays, up to $80 in United TravelBank cash for qualifying Avis or Budget rentals and up to $150 in annual JSX statement credits.

The Explorer offers similar credits for hotel stays, rental cars and JSX flights, but with lower annual allowances.

I've received some value from Quest's Instacart credit, and while it's nice to save a little on an online grocery order each month, it's not a perk that significantly affects how I value the card.

These credits could help justify the Quest's additional $200 in annual fees if you'll actually use them. Otherwise, I wouldn't give them too much weight in your decision, especially since some have specific booking requirements.

While the offers several advantages over the , upgrading won't make sense for everyone.

If you rarely check a second bag, don't fly United frequently enough to use the $200 annual TravelBank cash or aren't working toward Premier status, the Explorer may offer everything you need at a lower annual fee.

Both cards also share several benefits, including priority boarding, no foreign transaction fees and a credit of up to $120 for Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus every four years.

Before upgrading, I'd also consider whether applying for the Quest as a new card makes more sense, since you generally won't receive a welcome offer through a product change.

New cardholders can currently earn up to 90,000 bonus miles and 500 PQP: 500 PQP after their first purchase, 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening and an additional 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

However, if you're over Chase's 5/24 limit, you may not be eligible to open a new Chase card. In that case, upgrading could be worth considering if the Quest's benefits are a good fit for you.

Depending on your travel habits, it might also make sense to hold both cards. TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak is considering this strategy. She has the United Explorer and appreciates it for its lounge access, but believes she can also get substantial value from the Quest's various United perks.

If you're ready to upgrade from the to the , you'll need to call the number on the back of your credit card. Explain to the representative that you want to upgrade your card to the Quest Card.

Be clear with the agent on the phone that you want to change to the new card to ensure that Chase doesn't process a new card application or close your current card by mistake.

You should be able to continue using your current card until the new one arrives in the mail.

Related: The ultimate guide to credit card upgrades

The is a solid option for occasional United flyers, while the offers additional benefits that can make its higher annual fee worthwhile for frequent travelers.

If you regularly check bags, can use the annual TravelBank cash and value the Quest's other perks, upgrading could make sense. Otherwise, you may be better off sticking with the Explorer.

#6099. Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Points With 80% Bonus (1.1 Cents Each): Worth It?

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is currently offering a best-ever promotion on purchased points. Through December 31, 2026, Flying Club members can purchase points with up to an 80% bonus, which is potentially an opportunity to buy points for under 1.1 cents each. Suffice it to say that this could be a very attractive deal.

Link: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus

Between 12AM GMT on November 24 and 11:59PM GMT on December 31, 2026, the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club program is offering a bonus on purchased points. Virgin Atlantic is offering a tiered bonus of up to 80%, as follows:

Note that the purchase of Virgin Atlantic points is non-refundable, and purchasing points doesn’t count toward Flying Club elite status. Points will be credited to accounts within 24 hours, though they typically post faster than that, and almost instantly.

The cost to purchase Virgin Atlantic points varies based on where your account is registered:

The pricing is much better for those with accounts registered in the UK rather than the US. Assuming you’re eligible for an 80% bonus:

So as you can see, in the United States you can potentially pay 1.39 cents per point, while in the UK you can potentially pay 1.09 cents per point.

It’s interesting how much Virgin Atlantic penalizes those in the United States when it comes to buying points. Then again, when it comes to overall points earning opportunities, we can’t really complain in the United States, given the amazing credit card offers we have.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club ordinarily lets members purchase up to 200,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been doubled, to 400,000 points.

When Virgin Atlantic Flying Club offers a promotion on purchased points, the best version of the offer is almost always for a 70% bonus. As you can tell, this offer is even better than those, as this is truly a best-ever offer. Personally, I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a short term use in mind, rather than based on the slight difference in the cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Flying Club program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Flying Club points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

Nowadays Virgin Atlantic has dynamic award pricing for its own flights, and for those with flexibility who want the best deal, this can make for some great deals. For example, there are some transatlantic one-way business class awards that cost under 30,000 points, which is amazing.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 52,500-60,000 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Flying Club points to be worth 1.1 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Flying Club points than that.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points don’t expire. There’s no requirement to even have any account activity, as the points will never expire regardless.

While buying Virgin Atlantic points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Flying Club points. Most significantly, Virgin Atlantic is partners with major transferable points currencies, including American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou, and in all cases, points can be moved at a 1:1 ratio. There are several ways to earn these points aside from outright buying them.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is offering members an 80% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for 1.09-1.39 cents each (in USD), depending on where your account is registered.

There are plenty of circumstances where this could be a great deal. The only major consideration is that there are lots of other ways to earn Virgin Atlantic points with transferable points currencies, so some may prefer to earn rewards that way. With a specific use in mind, there could definitely be huge value in buying Flying Club points.
